As markets reassess U.S. inflation risks, global financial markets have once again experienced volatility at the start of the year. In February, global equities retreated sharply from their early-January peaks, erasing the significant gains posted at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equity markets have continued to rise amid low volatility, driven by expectations of sustained robust economic growth alongside an ideal environment of low inflation and interest rates. However, this expectation faces risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar has weakened, yet market operations continue to remain orderly. In the second half of 2017, total lending continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. After a modest slowdown in the previous year, both the rate of increase in property prices and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to the volatility of capital flows into and out of Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, ongoing normalization of U.S. monetary policy, and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant regarding heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and the elevated burden of household debt, banks should assess the potential impact of interest rate increases exceeding expectations on asset quality. After the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) lingered at low levels for over two years, global financial markets have once again experienced volatility at the start of the year. Global equities plummeted from their early-January peaks, with the S&P 500 falling more than 10% at one point, completely erasing the significant gains recorded at the start of the month. Market sentiment has shifted, as there are signs that the global economic recovery may pressure U.S. wages and prices, which have remained subdued for an extended period, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its rate-hiking pace. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield also climbed to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global stock markets have experienced a sustained upward trend, underpinned by market expectations of continued favorable economic conditions. In the second half of 2017, global economic momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity in both advanced and emerging market economies recovering in tandem. As the year drew to a close, the U.S. Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and comprehensive overhauls of both corporate and individual tax codes, fueling market expectations that the robust U.S. economic recovery would soon receive additional cyclical stimulus. Despite an intensification of activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remains subdued, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates will remain low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets surged notably in 2017, with U.S. equities repeatedly setting new highs. However, as the United States released January wage growth data that exceeded expectations, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. Following short-term financial market volatility, the risk of a tightening global monetary stance may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the United States, the economy has already reached its potential output; anticipated tax cuts aimed at providing cyclical stimulus to domestic demand could accelerate a rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more rapidly. At the same time, tax cuts are expected to widen the fiscal deficit, prompting the United States to issue more Treasury securities in the future. This is likely to intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to normalize its balance sheet. Outside the United States, growth momentum in other major advanced economies has strengthened, leading markets to anticipate that their central banks may scale back quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this move would lead to a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Tensions in international politics and geopolitics, along with the resulting policy and event risks, could also cast a shadow over the global economic growth outlook. The U.S. government appears to be increasingly inclined to adopt protectionist trade measures to shield domestic industries from competition, as recently demonstrated by the imposition of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminum. These actions raise concerns that trading partners may respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could disrupt global trade and intensify volatility in global financial markets. Given the aforementioned uncertainties in the global economic outlook, it remains questionable whether the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. At a fundamental level, it remains to be seen whether cyclical global demand growth and expectations of US tax cuts, which are driving up fiscal deficits, will raise the natural rate of interest (r*). Moreover, the Federal Reserve's normalization of its balance sheet is expected to increase term premiums, potentially lifting long-term interest rates and thereby weighing on asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies are also benefiting from an ideal environment characterized by robust growth and moderate inflation. With robust economic performance and optimistic outlooks, capital has accelerated its inflow, propelling financial markets higher. However, the favorable outlook outlined above faces downside risks from several factors: the synchronized normalization of monetary policy by major central banks, which has tightened global liquidity; the U.S. government's adoption of inward-looking trade policies; escalating geopolitical tensions; and the substantial repatriation of profits by U.S. corporations in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform, which could strain offshore U.S. dollar liquidity. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, with sectors and economies carrying high leverage levels being the most vulnerable to tightening financial conditions. Mainland China's economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure investment, and a rebound in industrial spending as the year drew to a close. At the same time, signs of the emergence of a "new economy" are becoming increasingly evident. Over the past few quarters, high value-added sectors such as manufacturing and services have demonstrated robust momentum in business expansion. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist. In particular, to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressures on growth posed by the further advancement of structural reforms remains to be seen. In 2018, the authorities on the mainland announced their continued commitment to an expansionary fiscal policy stance, which could help mitigate adverse economic developments when necessary. During the review period, progress was made in both structural reforms and the management of systemic risks. In particular, with the implementation of tightening measures, China's domestic real estate market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in the first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks have tightened their lending approval standards, their exposure to enterprises in overcapacity sectors remains under control, while shadow banking activities have also slowed amid the financial deleveraging drive. In addition to the positive developments noted above, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints appear to have tightened for state-owned enterprises (SOEs) with weaker repayment capacities, likely due to a reduction in support from local governments (see Special Topic 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid stabilizing economic conditions and reduced risks, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. Hong Kong's economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 3.8% in full-year 2017, marking the fastest pace in nearly six years. Private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017, supported by strong employment and income conditions, as well as rising asset prices. Total investment expenditure rebounded, driven by an increase in corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance further improved, benefiting from the upturn in global trade growth and the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism sector. Nevertheless, because the growth rate of imports outpaced that of exports, net goods exports weighed on GDP growth, while net services exports made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Private consumption, property and construction activities, and exports will continue to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates are ultimately expected to rise, Issue 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The government and the market consensus project 2018 real GDP growth at between 3% and 4%, and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the mainland's economic performance amid tighter financial conditions, as well as trends in the local asset markets, as mentioned above. Although the unemployment rate has fallen to a 20-year low of 2.9%, domestic inflation pressures remain under control. However, there have been slight signs of an uptick in the momentum of month-on-month inflation over recent months. Among these, prices for both tradable goods and services rose. Looking ahead, the core inflation rate is expected to rise slightly to remain at a moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rent increases in newly signed private residential leases. Tighter liquidity conditions, driven by funding requirements from new share issuance activities and seasonal cash needs, led to an increase in closing out of short positions in Hong Kong dollars, which in turn strengthened the HKD spot exchange rate between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate began to weaken again from December 2017. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets—particularly in equity markets—the Hong Kong dollar remained largely stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Exchange Rate Undertaking was not triggered. The Hong Kong Dollar Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) faced upward pressure between September and December 2017. This is primarily due to the funding requirements of new share issuance activities and banks' prudent approach to liquidity management as year-end approaches. In December, the average overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points, respectively, compared to six months earlier, reaching 0.25% and 1.26%. After a slight decline in early January 2018, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) have remained broadly stable and have not been affected by the recent adjustments in global financial markets. Despite fierce competition in the mortgage market, banks' average interest rates on new mortgage loans continued to rise in line with the upward trend in the short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offer rate, reaching 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banking funding costs remained generally low despite a brief uptick in October due to new share issuance activities, with the blended interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as U.S. monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face increased upward pressure; should global financial market sentiment shift abruptly, capital flow volatility could rise. In 2017, total bank loans increased steadily by 16.1% for the full year. Following robust growth of 10.2% in the first half, the pace of loan expansion slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Among these, the growth rates of both local loans and loans utilized outside Hong Kong have declined across most sectors. Growth in foreign-currency lending has slowed, partly due to rising dollar financing costs. Conversely, owing to the favorable local economic conditions and relatively low financing costs in Hong Kong dollars, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly. Due to loan growth in Hong Kong dollars outpacing deposit growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% by year-end, its highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, due to the relatively modest growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% by year-end. Both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilization between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar depreciated significantly against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. The Hong Kong offshore renminbi fund pool (comprising the total of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) experienced a slight decline in the first half of the year, followed by a modest rebound in the second half, broadly reflecting shifts in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore RMB businesses, while RMB loans continued to decline, the volume of RMB trade settlements processed by Hong Kong banks rebounded in the second half of the year. The average daily transaction value of the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) remains at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is poised to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the ongoing internationalization of the renminbi.

The synchronized global economic recovery that has gained momentum since late 2016 shows no signs of weakening. Improved growth prospects propelled global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, as markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States, global equity markets experienced a wave of selling and significant volatility in February, marking the end of the calm that had prevailed in financial markets over the past two years. Looking ahead, the risks of tightening global financial conditions, alongside a range of policy and event-related uncertainties, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. In a tight labor market, tax cuts in the United States could accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to hasten the pace of monetary tightening. As the Federal Reserve continues to normalize its balance sheet, the U.S. issuance of additional Treasury securities to fund tax cuts could intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The resurgence of trade barriers and the shadow they cast, along with the potential for unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions, could pose a threat to the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, robust export performance and steady domestic demand drove continued growth in real economic activity during the second half of 2017. However, while the economic outlook remains optimistic, it is also exposed to various downside risks, including potentially tighter-than-expected global monetary conditions, the United States' inward-looking trade policies, and escalating geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialize, they would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges: on one hand, they must guard against risks to economic growth, and on the other, they must curb the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet fragility. In mainland China, economic performance in the second half of 2017 was robust. During the review period, progress was made in structural reforms and in containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist. These will partly depend on the extent to which the rapid expansion of the "new economy" can offset the short-term growth pressures arising from further implementation of structural reforms. Due to a stabilizing economic environment and diminishing risks, pressure from capital outflows remained moderate for most of 2017. Since late 2016, as the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has solidified, growth in both advanced and emerging market economies has accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the United States experienced robust growth in investment and exports, buoyed by optimism in the private sector and a sharp depreciation of the U.S. dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilization of global commodity prices and rising import demand in major advanced economies. In the short term, following tax reform in the United States, investment and consumption are expected to gain further momentum from reductions in corporate and individual income taxes. Amid the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth will accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: Forecast of Real GDP Growth. As growth momentum strengthens in the euro area and Japan, market expectations point to a narrowing divergence in global monetary policy. Coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, this is boosting risk appetite and triggering capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby exerting downward pressure on the US dollar. Although the Federal Reserve raised interest rates three times during the year and began normalizing its balance sheet, the US Dollar Index still declined by nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite a broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies has remained weak and below central banks' targets, leading markets to expect, until recently, that global interest rates would remain low (Figure 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise through 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 repeatedly setting new highs. This propelled the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the early-2000s dot-com bubble. Figure 2.2: Core inflation in major advanced economies. However, since the second half of 2017, concerns have grown that tax cuts will widen fiscal deficits and fuel inflation, driving a sustained rise in U.S. long-term Treasury yields. Consequently, the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations has come into question. Following the release of U.S. data showing that average hourly wage growth in January 2018 exceeded expectations, markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States, triggering a correction in global stock markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index fell more than 10% from its January 26 peak, erasing the significant gains posted at the start of the year, and continued to come under pressure following the U.S. government's announcement of a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield also rose in mid-February to its highest level in four years. Market volatility surged sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) briefly climbing to a two-year high of 37.3, signaling the end of the narrow-range trading environment that had persisted over the past two years (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3: The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) outlook indicates that, following short-term equity market volatility, risks related to U.S. inflation, upward pressure on U.S. long-term Treasury yields, and potential monetary tightening by other major central banks could all contribute to tighter global financial conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, regarding the risks of U.S. inflation, the recently enacted tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The primary measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and individual income tax rates; (2) temporarily permitting full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision designed to reduce the incentive for U.S. corporations to retain overseas earnings abroad. Although it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the U.S. economy already at its potential output, the tax cuts could push U.S. output beyond potential levels, thereby triggering an overheating economy and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If the rise in inflationary pressures exceeds expectations, it could prompt the Federal Reserve to accelerate the tightening of monetary policy. Currently, financial market expectations for the federal funds rate path are more gradual than the trajectory projected by the Federal Reserve. However, should inflation unexpectedly rebound, the risk of a sudden reassessment of hiking expectations cannot be ruled out (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4: Federal Funds Rate Forecast. Furthermore, given that tax reform may exacerbate the fiscal deficit, the issuance of U.S. Treasury securities is expected to increase in the future. As the Federal Reserve continues its balance sheet normalization, term premiums are expected to rise; in this context, an increase in U.S. Treasury issuance could further intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Moreover, as market expectations for the passage of a U.S. tax-cut package have risen since the second half of 2017, inflation expectations in the United States have continued to increase (Figure 2.5). Consequently, after hovering near historic lows for most of 2017, the yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, reflecting in part market concerns over increased supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Figure 2.55: Five-year forward inflation expectations. Moreover, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (r*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain at low levels for an extended period as most analysts anticipate. Although estimates of the natural rate of interest (r*) vary, there is a broad consensus that it has declined significantly since the global financial crisis (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the US natural rate of interest (R*) may face upward risks in the future due to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate driven by rising fiscal deficits, and (2) potential increases in the investment rate stemming from corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment of capital expenditures. A rise in the R* rate, alongside expectations of the Federal Reserve normalizing its balance sheet, could lead to an increase in term premiums, potentially signaling higher long-term interest rates and thereby posing headwinds for asset market valuations. Figure 2.6 shows estimates of the natural rate of interest (r*) for the United States, the euro area, and Japan based on the Laubach-Williams model. Third, stronger growth momentum in the euro area and Japan has led markets to anticipate that their central banks may begin to scale back monetary easing measures. If such a scenario materializes, it may signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the euro area, all member economies have recorded a broad-based cyclical expansion (Figure 2.7). As for Japan, the economy is also accelerating its recovery, with real GDP posting its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continue to signal a commitment to accommodative monetary policy amid persistent inflationary weakness, the improving growth outlook for the Eurozone and Japan—coupled with ongoing tightening in Japan's labor market—has led some market participants to anticipate further reductions in their quantitative easing programs in the near future. Figure 2.7: The real GDP of select euro area member states, alongside policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions, may also threaten the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The U.S. government appears to favor inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries. Recent examples include the January 2018 announcement of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines, and the early March declaration of tariffs on steel and aluminum, raising concerns that trading partners may respond with retaliatory measures. At the same time, negotiations are ongoing between the UK and other EU countries regarding post-Brexit trade arrangements, with several uncertainties remaining throughout the process. Should the aforementioned developments lead to an increase in trade frictions, it could impede global trade flows and reduce global productivity. Furthermore, an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions—such as a military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East, or latent risks of terrorist attacks—could heighten volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, capping the year with robust performance. Actual growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, marking the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remains the primary driver of growth, while domestic demand continues to provide stable support (Figure 2.8). Accelerated recoveries in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in mainland China, and a resurgence in global demand for technology products have all boosted exports in the region. Figure 2.8 East Asia: Inflationary pressures from both domestic demand and exports remain subdued. In the second half of 2017, overall inflation in East Asia moderated, influenced by a decline in food price inflation and stable energy prices (Figure 2.9). At the same time, due to sluggish wage growth across multiple economies, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remains at a relatively low level. Figure 2.9 East Asia: Overall Core Consumer Price Inflation Rate* Note: Starting in 2016, the Republic of Korea set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/-0.5 percentage points. Source: CEIC and various central banks. A favorable economic outlook, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, drove a significant rise in financial asset prices in 2017 and the early part of 2018 (blue and pink bars in Figure 2.10). Capital inflows into the regional market rebounded sharply in 2017, with total securities investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. The valuation of various financial assets within the region also rose with the market. In fact, credit risk compensation in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while the region's benchmark equity index rose across the board. Currencies within the region generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With robust domestic demand and an improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Hong Kong's economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, threats to global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate, several upside risks persist. Hong Kong's economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, a rate comparable to the average growth of 0.9% recorded in the preceding two quarters (Figure 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily, remaining a key driver of GDP growth. Consumer spending grew steadily, driven by robust employment and income conditions, sustained consumer optimism, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, corporate capital expenditure increased, driving a significant rise in total investment expenditure in the final quarter after three quarters of relatively stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance further improved, benefiting from the upturn in global trade growth and the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism sector (Figure 3.2). Nevertheless, as the growth rate of imports exceeded that of exports, net goods exports weighed on GDP growth, while net services exports made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Figure 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions from major expenditure components. Figure 3.2: Sustained momentum in real export and import growth drove an increase in employment positions in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by approximately 0.7% to over 3.85 million during the period, with the most significant increases recorded in the construction, financial and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. Given that real gross domestic product growth outpaced employment growth, labor productivity showed further signs of improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to continue benefiting from an improving global economic outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Locally, private consumption is expected to continue growing, primarily driven by a robust labor market. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates are ultimately expected to rise, Issue 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. In terms of gross fixed capital formation locally, building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily, supported by an increase in housing supply and the continued rollout of infrastructure projects. While an improving economic environment will spur business capital expenditure, potential interest rate hikes could have a negative impact. The government forecasts real GDP growth in 2018 to be between 3% and 4%, while international institutions and private-sector analysts project growth in the range of 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the mainland's economic performance amid tighter financial conditions, as noted in earlier sections, as well as the trajectory of the local asset market. Local inflation pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although there have been slight signs of a rebound in month-on-month inflation momentum in recent months. On an annual comparison, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% in the third quarter and 1.6% in the fourth quarter, broadly in line with the average increase of approximately 1.7% recorded in the first half of the year. However, the core inflation rate, measured on an annualized basis over a three-month period and reflecting inflationary momentum, edged up slightly to 2.8% in January 2018 (Figure 3.3). Among these, prices for both tradable goods and services rose. The recovery in rents for newly signed private residential leases since mid-2016 may also have contributed, to some extent, to upward inflationary pressures (Figure 3.4). Moreover, labor cost pressures have continued to remain moderate over the recent quarters (Figure 3.5). Figure 3.3 illustrates various indicators of consumer price inflation; Figure 3.4 presents the Composite Consumer Price Index alongside its rental component and market rents; and Figure 3.5 shows unit labor costs and average earnings per employee. Given that global inflation remains subdued and domestic cost increases are stable, inflationary pressure in Hong Kong is expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate is likely to gradually recover from its eight-year low of 1.7% recorded in 2017. For instance, inflationary pressures may rise in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effect from rent increases in newly signed private residential leases. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation to be moderately 2.2% in 2018, while the government's projection for core inflation stands at 2.5%. Although inflation prospects remain moderate, upside risks persist. On the external front, any unexpected surge in global inflation or commodity prices could heighten domestic inflationary pressures. On the domestic front, the labor market has tightened further in recent times. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, marking the first time in nearly two decades that it has dipped below 3% (Figure 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; should the labor market tighten significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Figure 3.6: Unemployment rate. Following the 2008 global financial crisis, with interest rates remaining low, mortgage debt among Hong Kong households increased. As the normalization of U.S. interest rates advances, Hong Kong dollar rates will eventually rise in tandem, leading to an increased burden of mortgage repayments for households and, consequently, dampening household consumption. Accordingly, this study examines the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the proportion of mortgage servicing payments (comprising interest payments and principal amortization) relative to income. Figure B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution and income effects cited in standard economic theory, as well as the wealth and collateral effects arising from asset price fluctuations, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments, thereby changing households' disposable income, particularly for those with mortgage obligations. This impact will expand as the outstanding mortgage loan balance increases. Furthermore, the principal repayment amount on loans fluctuates with changes in the outstanding mortgage balance, which in turn affects private consumption by altering households' disposable income. Figure B3.1: Determinants of Private Consumption. To measure the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption, we estimated the ratio of outstanding mortgage repayments to income (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike the current debt-service-to-income (DSR) ratio, which applies only to newly originated mortgage liabilities, the Overall Mortgage Debt-to-Income Ratio (OMDSR) encompasses all outstanding household mortgage debt, which is more closely correlated with total private consumption. We largely adopted the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements to measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed-rate installments: Dt represents the outstanding residential mortgage loan balance in the banking sector; Yt denotes the aggregate income of owner-occupying households, calculated as the median income of owner-occupying households multiplied by the number of such households; and rt and st denote the average interest rate and loan term of the outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure mortgage repayment burdens across the entire household sector, it is advisable to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Figure B3.2 presents the OMDSR estimates for the period from 1985 to 2017, alongside the median ratios of mortgage repayments and loan repayments to income, as estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population censuses. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the decline in aggregate household mortgage borrowing and the significant drop in mortgage interest rates following the bursting of the 1997 property market bubble. Despite a sharp rise in property prices following the global financial crisis, these two ratios have remained stable, owing to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's macro-prudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which have curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of terms for newly originated mortgage loans has reduced the actual monthly mortgage payments. Figure B3.2: Median OMDSR and median debt-service-to-income ratios for mortgage repayments and loan repayments. We also compare the OMDSR with the banks' debt-service-to-income ratios, which represent the actual debt-service-to-income ratios of new mortgage applicants. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than the bank's contribution-to-income ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since property prices were lower at the time the original mortgages were granted, their monthly repayments are correspondingly lower than those of the new mortgages. Consequently, the debt servicing ratio for outstanding mortgages, which includes both existing and new loans (referred to as OMDSR), will be lower than the debt servicing ratio for new mortgages alone (i.e., the bank's loan-to-income ratio). Furthermore, the relatively higher loan-to-income ratio for banks stems from their adherence to the prudential regulatory requirements of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which mandate that non-mortgage loan repayments be factored into the loan-to-income ratio calculation. Following the global financial crisis, the Debt Servicing Ratio (DSR) for the Office of the Monetary Authority (OMDSR) and for banks remained stable, primarily due to the prudential regulation of mortgage loans implemented by the Monetary Authority. This regulation sets a cap on the mortgage debt servicing-to-income ratio for banks, which also helps to moderate the overall DSR. As illustrated in Figure B3.3, the newly originated mortgage debt servicing-to-income ratio for both the OMDSR and banks has remained stable overall. In general, the OMDSR aligns closely with conventional debt burden indicators; however, the OMDSR offers greater timeliness and reflects the debt burden associated with the entire stock of outstanding mortgage liabilities, rather than being limited to newly originated mortgage debts. Therefore, we believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of mortgage payment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on Hong Kong's private consumption, we estimate an error-correction model (ECM) following the methodologies of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (measured by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-run equation by an error-correction term. Drawing on existing theories and empirical evidence, we identify real income (measured by median household income, deflated by the Consumer Price Index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, and deflated by the Consumer Price Index), and the Old Age Disability and Survivors' Benefit (OMDSR) as long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has weakened, while the local interbank market continues to operate smoothly. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, though at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as U.S. monetary policy continues to normalize, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate may face increased upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment shifts dramatically, volatility in capital flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (see Figure 4.1). The spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar strengthened briefly from September to November 2017 and remained around the 7.80 level. This was primarily due to rising funding demands from new share issuance activities and banks' prudent approach to liquidity management toward month-end and year-end, which tightened overall liquidity conditions. Consequently, interest rate arbitrage activity slowed, while liquidation of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar increased. As Hong Kong dollar liquidity pressures eased and year-end commercial demand for US dollars rose, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, but the exchange guarantee was not triggered (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Figure 4.2: Capital flow indicator. The Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index experienced modest fluctuations in the second half of 2017 but is now facing increased downward pressure as the US dollar continues to weaken (Figure 4.3). This is broadly consistent with the trend of the US dollar against most major currencies. Given that the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners is narrow and has a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate (REER) index, the HKD's REER has continued to closely track the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) index. Figure 4.3: Net securities investment by non-residents showed an inflow in the second half of 2017, alongside the nominal and real effective exchange rates. The latest balance of payments statistics show that net inflows of equity securities investments by both local and non-local residents were recorded in the third quarter, reflecting an improved economic outlook in the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). In the third quarter of 2017, debt securities investment by non-residents recorded an inflow, offsetting the outflow of debt investment by residents. A survey of global mutual funds also revealed that, amid optimistic market sentiment regarding economic prospects and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investments recorded net inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, the survey data indicate that despite a correction in global financial markets, equity investments continued to see net inflows, while bond investments experienced modest net outflows (Figure 4.4). Figure 4.4 Market Survey Outlook on Fund Flows Related to Stocks and Bonds: Looking ahead, as the normalization of U.S. monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the U.S. dollar is expected to widen, potentially triggering an increase in arbitrage activity. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side exchange rate guarantee being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the linked exchange rate system. At the same time, given that the pace of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy normalization remains unclear and global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are subject to rapid shifts, volatility in Hong Kong dollar liquidity and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The Monetary Authority will continue to fully guarantee the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the currency board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve's rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodated in the second half of 2017 and recently. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base rose further by 1.4%, primarily driven by an increase in liability certificates issued for the issuance of banknotes (Figure 4.5). As the exchange guarantee was not triggered, the total surplus plus outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds remained largely unchanged in the second half of the year, standing at approximately HK$122.68 billion. Among these, the balance in the sum of reserves has decreased, while the outstanding Exchange Fund Notes and Bonds have correspondingly increased. This is due to the issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills, totaling HK$80 billion, to meet the substantial liquidity management needs of banks. Entering 2018, despite adjustments in the stock market, the monetary base remained stable. Figure 4.5: Components of the monetary base. Meanwhile, in the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar money supply continued to expand, albeit at a slower pace. The growth rate of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) decelerated from 8.9% in the first half of the year to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose marginally by 2.2% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly due to robust asset markets and rising investment demand. Asset analysis reveals that the growth in HKD M3 was supported on one hand by robust expansion in HKD loans (Figure 4.6), while on the other hand it was dampened by net outflows of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks' net foreign-currency assets. Figure 4.6: M3 in Hong Kong dollars and corresponding asset movements. On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits has been uneven. Partially reflecting a depreciation of the U.S. dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of U.S. dollar deposits declined from 3.0% in the first half of the year to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after declining for over two consecutive years, posted a significant rebound in the second half of the year, rising by 8.4%. This was primarily driven by the recent recovery in RMB deposits. Due to a slowdown in the growth of deposits denominated in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars, the total deposits of authorized institutions increased marginally by 3.0% in the second half of the year, compared with a 5.6% growth rate in the first half. For the full year of 2017, total deposits grew modestly by 8.7%, broadly in line with 2016. Figure 4.7: Deposit growth. Between September and December 2017, the demand for funds from initial public offering (IPO) activities increased, while banks adopted a prudent approach to liquidity management at month-ends and year-end. This exerted upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar interbank offer rate (Figure 4.8). Compared with six months ago, overnight and three-month Hong Kong interbank offered rates rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (based on monthly averages). The negative spread between the 1-month to 3-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates also narrowed accordingly. Figure 4.8: Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates versus the US dollar. At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly mirroring the trajectory of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half of the year, the yield on three-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds increased by a smaller margin of 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at year-end (Figure 4.9). Figure 4.9: Government bond yields, composite rates, and average mortgage interest rates on new loans. As 2018 began, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, the Hong Kong interbank offered rate (HIBOR) declined in early January. Subsequently, despite adjustments in both global and local equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate remained broadly stable. As of late February 2018, the overnight and three-month Hong Kong interbank offered rates closed at 0.43% and 1.08%, respectively. On the retail front, although bank loan rates have risen in line with the increase in Hong Kong's interbank offered rates, financing costs for banks have generally remained low due to the still substantial deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage market, the average interest rate on new mortgages issued by banks rose gradually by 36 basis points in December to 2.16% (Figure 4.9), broadly following the upward trend in the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR). On the other hand, although the composite interest rate used to gauge the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks rose briefly in October due to heightened capital-raising demands from new share issuances, it remained subdued for most of the second half of the year, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as the US Federal Reserve continues to normalize its monetary policy and other major economies may also begin to normalize interest rates, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate could face increased upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase volatility in capital flows. However, the substantial HKD monetary base can serve as a buffer, helping to moderate an overly rapid rise in HKD interest rates. Moreover, prudent liquidity management by banks, together with the ability to discount bills through the discount window, also helps to curb excessive volatility in interbank lending rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth reached 10.2% in the first half of the year, before slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Figure 4.10). In the second half of 2017, growth in loans used both within Hong Kong and outside Hong Kong moderated. By currency, owing to the improving local economic environment and relatively low financing costs in Hong Kong dollars, HKD-denominated loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans increased only marginally by 0.1%. Among these, growth in USD-denominated loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising costs of USD financing. In 2017, total loans grew robustly by 16.1%, compared with a 6.5% increase in 2016. Figure 4.10: The growth rate of loans in use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) declined from 9.4% in the first half of the year to 5.6% in the second half, with varying performance across major sectors (Figure 4.11). Growth in loans to the construction industry and for property development and investment slowed in the second half of the year, partly due to regulatory measures implemented since June 2017 requiring banks to strengthen risk management for lending to property developers. Despite further improvements in commodity trade and retail sales, loans to the trade finance and transport sectors recorded only modest growth, while lending to the wholesale and retail sectors declined. In contrast, loan growth in finance-related enterprises remains robust, reflecting, to some extent, the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Figure 4.11: Household Debt Growth by Individual Sector. Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with a 5.0% increase in the first half. Within household debt, private loans—including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes—saw an accelerated growth rate, rising by 12.4% in the second half of the year. The robust growth in private lending was primarily driven by borrowings from private banking and wealth management clients secured against financial assets. The growth in these loans is roughly in line with the sustained increase in client assets managed by the banks. The risks associated with such mortgages are manageable. In addition, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong issued guidance on private lending risk management to banks in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and debt service ratios for borrowers. On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the loan-to-value ratios of newly approved mortgages declined, resulting in a slight slowdown in the growth rate of residential mortgage loans to 3.8% in the second half of the year. Overall, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Figure 4.12).

Retail banking profits improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016, primarily driven by growth in net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions remain robust. After robust growth in the first half of 2017, credit expansion slowed in the second half, while asset quality remains sound by historical standards. Although the Hong Kong dollar interbank offering rate has risen significantly, retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs remain low due to the persistently low rates on retail deposits. However, banks should remain vigilant regarding the risks of rising interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows amid the normalization of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the persistent rise in corporate leverage and elevated levels of household debt, banks should assess the potential impact of interest rate increases exceeding expectations on asset quality. To enhance banks' resilience against systemic risks, Hong Kong's counter-cyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% effective January 1, 2019. In the second half of 2017, the retail banking division's pre-tax operating profit increased by 13.6% compared to the same period of the previous year. This was primarily driven by a significant increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the retail banking division's return on assets (ROA) dipped slightly from 1.17% in the first half of 2017 to 1.15% in the second half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Figure 5.1). For the full year 2017, the retail banking division's total pre-tax operating profit increased by 15.8%, while its return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Figure 5.1: Retail Bank Profitability. The net interest margin for retail banks widened further from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Figure 5.2). Evidence indicates that the improvement in net interest margins is consistent with the widening of average spreads on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Figure 5.3). Figure 5.2: Net interest margin of retail banks; Figure 5.3: Average spread on HKD syndicated loans. Since September 2017, the Hong Kong interbank offered rate has risen across the board, driven primarily by liquidity demands associated with initial public offerings and year-end bank funding needs, as well as expectations of U.S. interest rate hikes. The Hong Kong three-month interbank offered rate (HIBOR) reached 1.31% at the end of December 2017, its highest level since the global financial crisis, up 53 basis points from the end of June. Nevertheless, on a historical basis, this remains at a relatively low level (blue line in Figure 5.4). Entering 2018, with year-end liquidity demands from banks easing, Hong Kong interbank offered rates appeared to stabilize. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) has risen recently, the cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks has remained stable. This is mainly due to the low levels of retail deposit interest rates during the review period. In this context, the composite interest rate reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds in retail banking remained at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, rising only slightly to 0.38% by the end of December. (the green line in Figure 5.4). The overall cost of funds in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars for licensed banks in Hong Kong also exhibited a similar trend. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate held at around 2.8%, its lowest level in over two decades (Figure 3.6).
