On the other hand, if Sino-US trade tensions ease and local economic performance outperforms expectations, this could drive up domestic inflation. Figure 3.6: U.S. Unemployment Rate – The Sino-U.S. Trade Conflict Escalated in the Second Half of 2018: On July 6 and August 23, the United States imposed 25% tariffs on $34 billion and $16 billion worth of goods imported from mainland China, respectively. Following these two measures, China mainland also imposed a reciprocal 25% tariff on an equivalent value of U.S. goods in response. On September 24, the United States further escalated its measures by imposing an additional 10% tariff on $200 billion worth of goods imported from mainland China. China immediately retaliated by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on $60 billion worth of U.S. goods. Subsequently, the two countries initiated negotiations to prevent further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the imposition of additional tariffs is bound to have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the China-US trade dispute holds significant implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic stability and financial system. This专题 reviews Hong Kong's recent goods trade performance and explores its near-term outlook. We will also endeavor to utilize more granular data to distinguish trade goods directly affected by the imposition of additional tariffs, thereby enabling a more detailed assessment of their impact. To analyze the impact of tariffs, we first extracted six sets of Hong Kong re-export data, each corresponding to the successive rounds of tariff hikes described in the preceding section. In the first two rounds of tariff increases, the United States primarily imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, whereas Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the scope of affected goods expanded to include more consumer products. For the sake of brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of additional tariffs as List 1, List 2, and List 3, respectively. After collecting these more detailed trade data, we focus on analyzing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong's re-exports to adjust for seasonal factors. Additionally, readers should exercise caution when analyzing September 2018 data, as trade activities in that month were to some extent disrupted by the super typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings of this section should be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of additional tariffs. Shortly after additional tariffs were imposed on Hong Kong re-exports originating from mainland China and subject to tariff impacts, the volume of goods transiting from mainland China through Hong Kong to the United States appeared to decline sharply or at least experience a marked slowdown (Figure B3.1). For instance, re-export growth on Lists 1 and 2 slowed in the first month following the imposition of additional tariffs, while re-exports on List 3 recorded negative growth. Furthermore, re-exports across all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Figure B3.1 shows the value of 2018 transshipments from mainland China to the United States via Hong Kong, where the goods' country of origin was the United States and thus subject to tariffs. In contrast, transshipments from the United States to mainland China via Hong Kong exhibited different patterns (Figure B3.2). The transshipment under List 1 appeared to decline sharply within a few months after the imposition of additional tariffs, yet it rebounded as the year drew to a close. Re-exports in List 2 were broadly in negative growth for the full year, while growth in List 3 appeared relatively stable. Figure B3.2: Value of goods re-exported from the United States via Hong Kong to mainland China in 2018, showing front-loading. Due to the time lag between the announcement of tariffs and their implementation (or due to the mere threat of additional tariffs), firms may accelerate shipments of affected goods ahead of the anticipated effective date of the tariffs. In fact, both data and news reports indicate that such advance shipment practices are quite prevalent. Some private-sector analysts also believe these actions were a contributing factor to the robust overall trade figures ahead of the tariff hikes. More granular trade data indicate some evidence of advance shipments for certain tariff-listed goods, though this appears to be limited to goods transiting from mainland China to the United States (Figure B3.1). The re-export growth rates for List 1 and List 2 both increased in the several months preceding the implementation of their respective tariffs. On the other hand, the growth rate of transshipment from the United States via Hong Kong to mainland China (Figure B3.2) does not indicate a significant pattern of advance shipments by enterprises. Notably, re-exports through Hong Kong unaffected by additional tariffs constitute the majority, while those directly impacted account for only approximately 4% to 5% of the total value of Hong Kong's re-exports. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports that are unaffected by additional tariffs. We found that transshipment not affected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Figure B3.3). Furthermore, the decline in re-export growth affected by tariffs (red line) has become markedly steeper since the third quarter, underscoring the significant impact of tariffs. The slowdown in re-export growth unaffected by additional tariffs partly reflects a broader weakening of external demand. Amid escalating trade frictions, which are heightening uncertainty, tightening global financial conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, external demand may face broader downward pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in corrections across major stock markets. Weaker import demand in other economies has consequently weighed on Hong Kong's external trade performance. Figure B3.3: 2018 Re-export Values in Hong Kong. Even with a moderation in US-China trade tensions, Hong Kong's short-term prospects for goods trade remain challenging. Global growth is expected to moderate in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further constrain Hong Kong's export performance. Business climate indicators across sectors reveal that both large and small enterprises hold a pessimistic outlook on their business prospects (Figure B3.4), with the trading sector experiencing particularly subdued sentiment. Other trade-related sectors, such as logistics, may also be affected. Figure B3.4: Business outlook survey of Hong Kong's import and export industries.

The Hong Kong dollar strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting tighter liquidity driven by anticipated seasonal funding demand, which triggered unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar gradually weakened, partly due to corporations repatriating funds raised through new equity issuances and the market rebuilding carry-trade positions, triggering the weak-side convertibility guarantee in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong interbank offered rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before declining in January 2019. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the continued US-China trade friction, the Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization, capital flows in the Hong Kong dollar may become more volatile. If the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the United States remains wide, carry trades are likely to persist, keeping the Hong Kong dollar weak over the near term and potentially triggering the weak-side convertibility guarantee, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the weak-side exchange guarantee in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side exchange guarantee was triggered again in March 2019, a total of four times as of March 19 (Figure 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate experienced a brief rise in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, before gradually declining in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilized again after November, as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity, triggering the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, reflecting partly the repatriation of proceeds from new share issuances by corporations and the market's rebuilding of carry trade positions. Following the widening of the US-HK interest rate differential after year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, gradually weakening the HKD and triggering the weak-side exchange rate guarantee in March. Despite the activation of the weak-side conversion guarantee, HKD trading continued smoothly and orderly. The surplus has remained at approximately HK$76 billion since August (Figure 4.2), dipping slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side exchange rate guarantee in March (as of March 19). The net outflow of Hong Kong dollars since April 2018 represents only a small fraction of the approximately HKD 1 trillion that has flowed into the territory since 2008. Figure 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Figure 4.2: Capital flow indicator. The Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index has generally followed movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Figure 4.3). Given the narrow inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which has had a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate (REER) index, the REER index has largely followed the trajectory of the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) index. Figure 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates  Latest Balance of Payments Statistics indicate that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amidst a sluggish market sentiment and heightened volatility in the stock market, outflows of equity securities investments by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting the inflows of securities investments by non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investments by both local residents and non-local residents recorded net inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization, capital flow volatility may intensify. Furthermore, a significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar could spur arbitrage trading activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the linked exchange rate system, the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate could weaken, potentially triggering the weak-side conversion guarantee once again. Capital outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side convertibility guarantee are both normal operational features of the linked exchange rate system. Despite the ongoing normalization of U.S. interest rates and the multiple triggers of the weak-side exchange rate guarantee between April and August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base contracted marginally by 0.7% in the second half of the year, amounting to HK$163.29 billion by the end of 2018 (Figure 4.4). The contraction of the monetary base was primarily attributable to the activation of the weak-side exchange rate guarantee in August 2018, which reduced the aggregate balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion by the end of 2018. Meanwhile, liabilities in the form of banker's acceptances, government-issued banknotes and coins, and outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds increased marginally. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant changes in the total since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee in March, the total surplus declined slightly to approximately HK$70.9 billion as of March 19. Figure 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. In relation to broader HKD monetary supply indicators, the growth rate of the money supply generally decelerated in the second half of the year, reflecting in part an increase in uncertainty in the macroeconomic and financial environment. The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year, but increased only marginally by 0.1% in the second half (Figure 4.5). As the major component of HKD M3, HKD deposits showed little change compared to the end of June (Figure 4.6). In Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly due to a reduction in investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; meanwhile, term deposits continued to register robust growth, driven by an increase in deposit interest rates. Asset analysis indicates that the slowdown in growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was due to changes in bank capital and reserves, which are included in the "net other items" category. Figure 4.5: Changes in the components of Hong Kong dollar M3. Foreign currency deposits accelerated their growth in the second half of the year. Following an increase in preferential interest rates on US dollar deposits, banks attracted higher deposit volumes, leading to a robust 8.8% year-on-year growth in US dollar deposits in the second half of the year, which became the primary driver of overall foreign currency deposit growth (Figure 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased modestly by 1.4% in the second half of the year, with renminbi deposits continuing to grow. Overall, total deposits at authorized institutions rose modestly by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase recorded in the first half. Figure 4.6: Deposit Growth. Despite the still-substantial size of the Hong Kong dollar monetary base and deposits, the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate began to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018, primarily reflecting the U.S. interest rate hikes. Seasonal working capital demands occasionally push up short-term interbank rates, resulting in greater volatility for these rates compared to long-term interbank rates (Figure 4.7). The average Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) for 3-month and 12-month tenors in December was 2.32% and 2.74%, respectively, approximately 30 basis points higher than the June averages. Entering 2019, amid a seasonal decline in demand, the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate (HIBOR) fell overall. The average values for the 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) in February fell to 1.65% and 2.39%, respectively. Figure 4.7: The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) interbank offer rate (IBOR) yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly following movements in the U.S. dollar yield curve. Compared to the end of June 2018, yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bonds declined by 45 and 37 basis points, respectively, to 1.56% and 1.83% by the end of February 2019 (Figure 4.8). Figure 4.8: Review of Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average New Mortgage Loan Rates. During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting fluctuations in interbank and deposit financing costs, the blended interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% by the end of December 2018, before declining to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Figure 4.8). Amid rising financing costs, following the Federal Reserve's September increase in the target range for the federal funds rate, retail banks raised their prime lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. Following a further increase in the U.S. federal funds rate target range in December, retail banks have not adjusted their prime lending rates again. On the other hand, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans followed the rise in the prime lending rate, reaching approximately 2.45% by the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the trajectory of US interest rates, capital flows, and local financial market activities (such as initial public offering subscription activity) will continue to be the primary drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given the substantial size of the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) monetary base and the large holdings of Exchange Fund bills by the banking system, the pace of HKD interest rate increases should remain moderate, as banks can pledge these bills as collateral to borrow HKD funds through the discount window. Amidst intensifying trade friction between China and the United States, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have depreciated against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Figure 4.9). However, buoyed by the optimism following the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the United States, both the offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates stabilized in November. At the same time, the spread between onshore and offshore renminbi remained insignificant during the review period. Figure 4.9: Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates. At present, the ongoing U.S.-China trade friction has not yet significantly impacted liquidity conditions in the offshore interbank market. Given that liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore Renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate (HIBOR) stayed below 4% for most of the review period, with only occasional upticks driven by seasonal factors (Figure 4.10). The three-month offshore Renminbi interbank rate hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, then fell to 3.02% by the end of February 2019, likely reflecting the People's Bank of China's recent monetary easing measures. Nevertheless, the impact of the progress in US-China trade negotiations on the liquidity of the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Figure 4.10: Overnight and 3-Month CNH Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) Pricing. Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The balance of RMB customer deposits and deposit certificates grew slightly faster than the 2.6% increase recorded in the first half of the year, rising by 3.7% in the second half to reach RMB 657.7 billion by the end of 2018 (Figure 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was primarily driven by RMB customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half of the year and by 5.2% in the second half. The growth rate of corporate customer deposits outpaced that of individual customer deposits. However, the outstanding balance of certificates of deposit (CDs) declined by an additional 14.1% in the second half of the year, primarily due to reduced issuance of CDs and a relatively higher volume of CDs maturing in October.

Retail banking profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared to the same period in 2017, primarily driven by an increase in net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions remain robust. Reflecting upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank lending rates and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, the overall funding costs for retail banks in Hong Kong have risen significantly, yet remain at a relatively low level. In the context of an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilizing since November, and asset quality remains robust by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to ongoing uncertainty in China–US trade relations, a global economic slowdown, an unclear pace of the U.S. monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the persistent rise in corporate leverage levels, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact of a further deterioration in the external environment on credit risks associated with their corporate loan portfolios. Pre-tax operating profit for retail banking grew by 14.3% compared to the same period in 2017, while return on assets increased from 1.14% to 1.23% (Figure 5.1). This strong performance was primarily driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the rise in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For the full year 2018, the retail banking segment's total pre-tax operating profit increased by 19.4%, while its return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Figure 5.1: Retail Bank Profitability. The net interest margin of the retail banking segment widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2 shows that the net interest margin of retail banks largely reflected the United States' further interest rate hikes and the decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side exchange rate guarantee in August 2018, resulting in continued upward pressure on Hong Kong interbank funding costs in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Figure 5.3). In response to banks' widespread increase in fixed deposit rates to secure long-term, stable funding, retail deposit rates in Hong Kong dollars also rose during the review period. Furthermore, following the US Federal Reserve's interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their prime lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate—a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banking—increased from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, yet remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Figure 5.3 Interest rates: (a) end-of-period figures. (b) The average number of new loans approved during the period. More broadly, the overall cost of funds in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars for licensed banks has continued to rise. In the second half of 2018, the average overall funding costs for Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits at banks rose by 36 basis points, compared to a 40 basis point increase in the first half (see the red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4: Funding Costs and Maturity Profile of Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funds for Licensed Banks. The cumulative increase in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) has outpaced the rise in overall funding costs for Hong Kong banks. This trend may have a positive impact on retail mortgage loans benchmarked to HIBOR, and the banking sector has actively promoted such loans in recent years. However, future improvement in net interest margins may become more constrained, as most mortgage loans benchmarked to the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) have already reached their upper interest rate caps tied to the best lending rate. Given the uncertainty regarding the timing of future increases in the most favorable loan rates, the continued rise in banks' funding costs amid the normalization of U.S. interest rates may place pressure on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, rising uncertainty in the external environment could cast a shadow on banks' profit outlook. Particularly against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, continued uncertainty in US-China trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this situation leads to a significant decline in lending and deterioration in asset quality, it could strain banks' profitability. Hong Kong's banking sector maintains robust capital adequacy, far exceeding international minimum standards. By the end of 2018, the combined capital adequacy ratio of locally registered authorized institutions further increased to 20.3% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% comprised Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Figure 5.5 Capital of Locally Registered Recognized Institutions: 1. Overall Status. 2. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to curb excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018. As of end-December 2018, the leverage ratio of locally registered authorized institutions stood at a robust 8.0%, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.6 shows the leverage ratio of locally registered recognized institutions, measured in accordance with the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement. The banking sector's liquidity position remained robust throughout the review period. The average liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) for Group 1 institutions increased from 156.6% in Q2 2018 to 167.6% in Q4 2018 (Figure 5.7), substantially exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio: 1. Overall Status. 2. Quarterly average figures. The average stable net funding ratio for Group 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Figure 5.8), significantly exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average core capital ratio for Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. Against a backdrop of persistent uncertainty in the US-China trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit expansion decelerated significantly in the second half of 2018. The coronavirus outbreak that erupted in early 2020 simultaneously struck both demand and supply, presenting global economic challenges distinct from previous crises. Although major central banks and several governments have implemented stimulus measures since early March to mitigate the economic shock caused by the pandemic, financial markets remain volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in both the global and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continue to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Against the backdrop of a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable aggregate balance, and a moderate increase in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. After a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, the growth rate of total loan disbursements slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, albeit with somewhat erratic trends. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face several downward risks stemming from uncertainties related to the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social developments. Given the continuing rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has begun to show signs of stabilization, bolstered by major central banks' enhanced monetary easing measures, a de-escalation of trade tensions between China and the United States, and a reduced risk of a no-deal Brexit. However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has sparked market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks posed by the pandemic, several major central banks significantly cut interest rates and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. However, tightening global financial conditions have resulted from widening credit spreads and a sharp decline in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will dampen global economic activity, with the extent of the impact depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners could again grow tense, while trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union following Brexit may prove fraught with difficulties. Persistently weak global demand continues to drag down economic growth in East Asia. Exports from East Asia to major destinations, including the United States, European economies, and mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecom equipment exporters in the region have recently reported revenue growth, though whether the technology product cycle is broadly rebounding remains to be seen. Financial markets responded positively to the China–U.S. Phase One trade agreement announced in December 2019, as the trade truce helped reduce global trade uncertainties to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds, including weak corporate profitability and elevated private-sector leverage. At the same time, the outbreak of the coronavirus has raised concerns that the region's economy could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans implemented by multiple economies within the region may deal a blow to Asia's tourism sector, particularly to those economies that are more reliant on tourism services exports. Given the region's close integration with supply chains on the Chinese mainland, the manufacturing sector may also be impacted by the outbreak. In mainland China, economic growth continued to decelerate in the second half of 2019, owing to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the US-China Phase One trade deal has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing China's economy, downward pressure persists amid the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing, and a slowdown in the global economy. The Central Economic Work Conference convened in December 2019 identified stabilizing the economy as the key priority for 2020, while simultaneously emphasizing the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that mainland China's economic growth will decelerate to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite relevant measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may face declining shareholder equity in recent years, a trend viewed as a sign of regression in the private sector. Special Topic 2, which analyzes 2018 data from listed companies to identify the drivers of changes in equity holdings of mainland industrial enterprises, finds that private enterprises and small firms are not inherently more susceptible to shrinkage or regression. Although research identifies negative profitability as the primary driver, other factors—particularly structural ones—also warrant attention (see Spotlight 2). Hong Kong's economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. The real gross domestic product has continued to decline over the past three quarters, indicating that Hong Kong's economy has entered a recession. Dragged down by these factors, the economy contracted by 1.2% in full-year 2019, a marked deterioration from the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018 and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down Hong Kong's GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social unrest has severely dampened consumer activity, leading to a weak economic outlook and eroding confidence among both consumers and businesses. In light of significant headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. Over the last ten years, intensified integration of global financial markets has led to a marked increase in cross-border securities investment capital flows worldwide. A recent study indicates that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment fund flows are driven by index-tracking funds. Index-driven funds encompass not only funds that closely track investment indices, commonly known as passive funds, but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices in their management strategies. 9. By attracting overseas investors that the respective emerging economies would otherwise be unable to draw or reach, these funds help advance the development of their financial markets. Accordingly, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, thereby fostering long-term growth and stability in their markets. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, market concerns suggest that such funds' investments may undermine the fiscal discipline of corporate bond issuers, potentially leading to elevated leverage levels. 10. Furthermore, some argue that the recent growth of index-tracking funds has exacerbated volatility in global securities investment flows, rendering emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by common shared drivers—more vulnerable. 11 This report assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital across the relevant bonds in proportion to their respective weights within the benchmark index. Consequently, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions characteristic of passive bond funds may diminish the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the best interests of fund investors. 13 Worse still, from the perspective of financial stability, such behavior may fuel excessive borrowing, exposing corporate sectors in emerging market economies—where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis—to significant credit and solvency risks (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1: Corporate leverage in emerging market economies. We estimate the exposure of corporate bond issuers in emerging markets to passive bond funds using each issuer's weight in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds.¹⁴ We find that an increase in such passive investment tends to raise the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the relevant corporate issuers. The blue solid bars in Figure B1.2 represent the estimated effects. In addition to promoting the development of corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the expansion of the long-term bond investor base through passive bond funds also benefits corporate development in these economies. We also find that the aforementioned effects are significant only for corporate firms in emerging market economies with more robust fundamentals—particularly those with stronger debt-servicing capacity and lower leverage ratios (represented by the green solid bars in Figure B1.2). Firms facing higher financial distress costs, particularly those with high leverage or weaker debt-servicing capacity, do not appear to be further drawn into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. In summary, the aforementioned studies indicate that the growth in passive bond fund investment may not substantially increase the debt-servicing risk for corporate sectors in emerging market economies.

Despite a noticeable slowdown in Hong Kong's economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8% to 2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. Against this backdrop, this paper analyzes recent developments in the labor market and provides a short-term outlook, including an examination of why the overall labor market remained broadly robust in the first three quarters of 2019, with the unemployment rate showing virtually no change, and the implications of this trend for future developments. It is worth noting that, in part due to the costs associated with adjusting labor demand, the unemployment rate serves as a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate typically lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). The Hong Kong dollar has strengthened since October, with upward momentum intensifying in December, further propelling the currency to remain within the strong side of the convertibility range over the past few months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar stems partly from stock-related needs and partly from the unwinding of short positions in the HKD as liquidity tightened toward year-end. Overall, the operation of Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets remains smooth and orderly. Despite an uncertain external environment and the potential for heightened capital flow volatility triggered by market sentiment shifts due to the coronavirus pandemic, Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand capital outflow pressures without compromising the stability of its financial sector. Supported by heightened demand for the Hong Kong dollar linked to equities, including initial public offerings, the HKD exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Figure 4.1). Entering December, upward momentum for the Hong Kong dollar strengthened further. From mid-December through February, the HKD exchange rate remained within the strong-side convertibility band. The Hong Kong dollar strengthened, driven in part by robust initial public offering activity and, in part, by the tightening of liquidity near year-end, which prompted the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased slightly, and the Hong Kong dollar depreciated modestly, closing at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, during the review period, the HKD trading market continued to operate smoothly and orderly. As no strong or weak exchange rate guarantee was triggered during the review period, the net balance remained unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Figure 4.2: Net surplus and Exchange Fund bills and bonds. The Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index largely followed movements in the US dollar, posting a slight increase over the review period (Figure 4.3). Given the narrow inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which has had a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate (REER), the REER has largely tracked the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER). Figure 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates When measuring Hong Kong's capital flows, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts: (1) HKD-denominated capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. The HKD fund flow analysis focuses on the currency dimension of fund flows, aiding the assessment of monetary stability, particularly under the linked exchange rate system. On the other hand, cross-border capital flows, which focus on the movement of funds across regions through Hong Kong's banking system, contribute to assessing the overall stability of Hong Kong's financial system. The two cash flow concepts require distinct monitoring indicators. When monitoring the flow of HKD funds, it is essential to pay attention to the HKD exchange rate and the total balance. If the public or investors were to significantly shift their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar would naturally decline, leading to a depreciation of its exchange rate. Under the linked exchange rate system, if the Hong Kong dollar weakens to the weak-side conversion rate of 7.85 HKD per US dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority stands ready to purchase Hong Kong dollars upon banks' requests, thereby reducing the monetary base. Since April 2019, the net surplus has remained broadly unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar has recently been trading near the strong-side convertibility guarantee. Consequently, no significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, the total amount of bank deposits in Hong Kong serves as a useful indicator. When substantial capital outflows occur in Hong Kong's banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflows. The operation of Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets remains smooth and orderly, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the territory's monetary environment remains limited. However, we must closely monitor the risks arising from the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system. The Monetary Authority has the capacity, resources, and resolve to address capital outflows and maintain the stability of Hong Kong's currency and financial system. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained substantial, rising by 4.0% since late June to HK$168.94 billion by the end of January 2020 (Figure 4.4). As no conversion guarantee was triggered during this period, the ending balance remained broadly unchanged at approximately HKD 54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds, certificates of indebtedness, as well as government-issued circulating banknotes and coins, have risen steadily. Figure 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, the broad HKD money supply indicator remained broadly stable.
