The rollout of novel coronavirus vaccines has offered hope for economic recovery and bolstered global growth prospects. Furthermore, sustained fiscal and monetary easing policies have propelled financial markets to record highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, with economic recoveries expected to proceed at uneven paces across economies. In the medium term, policymakers will face challenges stemming from the decoupling of financial markets from the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the enduring economic scars left by the pandemic. The operation of Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets remains smooth and orderly. The Hong Kong dollar has moved close to the strong-side convertibility peg, primarily driven by demand linked to equities. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant outflows of funds from the Hong Kong banking system. Partially reflecting the recurrence of the pandemic, which has weakened economic activity and reduced credit demand, total bank lending in the second half of the year declined slightly. However, on a full-year 2020 basis, lending still registered a modest increase. At the same time, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, the uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery, coupled with persistent geopolitical risks, will continue to pose challenges for Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may erode the repayment capacity of enterprises and households; therefore, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of these downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened worldwide, but resumed slowing from the fourth quarter onward amid a resurgence in coronavirus infections. Nevertheless, as vaccine development achieved a breakthrough by the end of 2020, market expectations grew that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, paving the way for the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Furthermore, sustained fiscal and monetary easing drove global financial markets to record highs in early 2021, even as signs of divergence from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to loom over the global economic outlook. Whether the vaccine can be widely distributed remains to be seen. At the same time, supply bottlenecks and the previously expansionary monetary policy could drive inflation above expectations, prompting central banks to tighten monetary policy ahead of schedule and thereby ending market expectations for a "longer period of lower interest rates." In the long term, policymakers must evaluate the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address numerous economic legacies stemming from the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and enduring economic trauma. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. As risk appetite improved, capital inflows into regional securities markets rebounded, and carry trades resurged. Despite the aforementioned positive developments, the East Asian region continues to face persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less-developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, thereby hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Secondly, variables in vaccine supply, coverage, and efficacy, combined with weakening fiscal conditions among governments in the region, could dampen market sentiment and trigger capital outflows. In mainland China, as consumer activities gradually returned to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. In 2020, China's economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to register positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains largely dependent on the evolution of the pandemic and shifts in U.S.-China tensions. The latest consensus forecast indicates that mainland China's economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months at the beginning of 2020, but subsequently strengthened for the remainder of the year amid an accelerating economic recovery, a weaker U.S. dollar, and robust capital inflows into mainland China's bond market. Detailed analysis shows that during the outbreak of the novel coronavirus, fundamental factors, rather than market sentiment, played a more significant role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Spotlight 1 for details). Hong Kong's economy showed improvement in the second half of 2020, yet real gross domestic product remained far below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight uptick in local demand and further expansion of exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending a five-quarter consecutive contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real gross domestic product narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to approximately 3% in the second half. However, the aggregate real GDP for the full year 2020 contracted by 6.1%, marking the largest decline on record and, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019, representing the first instance of two consecutive years of decline in history. Latest data on local GDP by industry indicate that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related sectors has been more severe than that of the overall economy during the pandemic. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the Government introduced two additional rounds of the Epidemic Prevention and Control Fund in the second half of 2020—the third and fourth rounds—to assist industries and residents affected by the outbreak and to strengthen Hong Kong's pandemic response capabilities. The Government has also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to stimulate the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of 100% guaranteed special personal loans for unemployed individuals. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), in collaboration with the Banking Industry SME Loan Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 that the "Interest-Only, Principal-Deferment" scheme would be extended until October of the same year, and also extended the repayment tenures for trade finance loans under the scheme. These deferral measures are expected to help alleviate the working capital difficulties faced by some corporate clients. The COVID-19 vaccine is expected to restore normal economic activity. The local economy is projected to achieve positive growth in 2021 on an annual basis; however, the strength and pace of the economic recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic, the rollout schedule of vaccines, and their efficacy. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, Mainland China's economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs. The government forecasts real GDP growth in 2021 to be in the range of 3.5% to 5.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private-sector analysts stands at 4.4%. Labor market conditions further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate continued to climb, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a level not seen since the SARS outbreak. To address the persistently deteriorating labour market, the Government introduced the "Employment Support Scheme" under the second round of the Pandemic Prevention and Control Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to help them retain their employees. Following the conclusion of the "Protect Jobs" scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Epidemic Prevention and Control Fund (such as one-off grants) to further support industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, given the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Topic 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and decline of Hong Kong's tourism industry on the local labor market. Domestic inflationary pressure continued to ease from mid-2020 through February 2021, over an eight-month period. The core consumer price inflation rate fell sharply on an annual basis to 0.3% in the third quarter and 0.2% in the fourth quarter of 2020, and further declined to -0.5% in January and -0.1% in February 2021. The underlying inflation rate, measured on an annualized basis over the past three months as an indicator of inflationary momentum, has remained at a relatively low level in recent months, despite slight fluctuations. Given the persistent challenges in the global and local economic environment, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to remain modest in the near term, particularly as the recent slowdown in private residential rental growth continues to restrain local inflation. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate in 2021 will be a moderate 1.4%, while the government projects basic and overall inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively, for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar has edged close to its strong-side convertibility bound, driven primarily by equity-related capital demand, including robust new share issuance activity and southbound fund inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Financing activity remained robust during the first two months of 2021, exerting upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. During the review period, the Strong Currency Peg was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in net inflows of HK$263.3 billion into Hong Kong dollars. The Strong Side Conversion Facility was triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar market continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. From a regional perspective, during the review period, the total deposit balance increased, indicating no signs of significant capital outflow from Hong Kong's banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic's trajectory, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions in China-US relations could exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand such volatility. As the Strong-End Exchange Rate Trigger was activated, leading to an increase in the Exchange Fund's closing balance, the Hong Kong dollar interbank offer rate generally remained at very low levels. The composite rate reflecting the average cost of HKD funding in retail banking declined further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Driven by lower funding costs, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of the major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. During most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore rate, with an average premium of approximately 100 basis points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. The offshore RMB liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to expand in the second half of 2020. By the end of January 2021, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit had risen to RMB 826.3 billion. As for other renminbi business, renminbi-denominated bank loans in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased. The daily average transaction volume of the renminbi real-time gross settlement system remained at a high level of RMB 1.1915 trillion throughout 2020. Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure offers investors numerous cross-border capital channels connecting to the mainland. With the continued opening of China's capital account, growing international demand for RMB-denominated assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Greater Bay Area framework, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit. Supported by the rise in global equity markets and robust buying of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors via the Stock Connect, the local stock market staged a rebound following a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global stock markets rose, driven by unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies, optimism about positive progress in vaccine development that could accelerate the recovery of economic activity, and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered after its sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% over the review period and briefly breaking through the 31,000-point level in mid-February 2021, reaching a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following a wave of significant net outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence rebounded swiftly as governments worldwide implemented unprecedented economic stimulus measures, triggering a recovery in inflows to local bond funds. Despite a modest rebound in yields over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remain near historic lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, market expectations point toward an eventual end to the novel coronavirus pandemic and accelerated global economic growth. Amid expectations of a more prolonged global monetary policy of low interest rates, investors were not deterred by the late-2020 pandemic resurgence, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the market's robust optimism is at odds with a still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should the economic recovery prove weaker than expected, or if policy support is withdrawn sooner than anticipated (for instance, due to inflation exceeding forecasts), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the challenge of determining when to withdraw policy support, while also addressing a range of lingering issues from the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-term economic trauma. The ongoing uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over economic recovery in East Asia, posing greater challenges for slower-developing emerging market economies in the region in terms of vaccine procurement and distribution. Any slowdown in the progress of the vaccination program could reverse current optimism, leading to volatile capital flows and financial market instability. In mainland China, as consumption activities gradually returned to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely dependent on the trajectory of the pandemic and the evolution of tensions between China and the United States. Accordingly, the government has announced its continued support for an accommodative policy stance, while emphasizing the importance of containing systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the economic reopening, major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, infection numbers from the novel coronavirus have risen again, prompting governments across the globe to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, thereby dampening the momentum of global growth once more. By the end of 2020, a more transmissible variant emerged, subsequently spreading globally and exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use by the end of 2020, market expectations have shifted toward the eventual end of the pandemic, a return to normalcy in the global economy, and accelerated growth. Another driver of global economic recovery has been sustained policy stimulus, including major central banks' commitment to "lower-for-longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, alongside continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages enacted by the U.S. Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised its global real GDP growth forecast for 2021 upward to 5.5%, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from the projection issued in October 2020 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: IMF real GDP growth forecasts as of January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market sentiment improved, with cyclical sectors typically benefiting from economic recovery posting share price gains, which drove global equity prices and valuations to record highs in early 2021 (Figure 2.2). Figure 2.2: Twelve-month forward P/E ratios of major stock indices. Nevertheless, while financial markets have performed strongly, the macroeconomic environment remains fraught with challenges; the divergence between the two could trigger volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the epidemic under control hinges on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the global vaccination rate remained low (Figure 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX have been established to promote more equitable vaccine distribution, the limited supply of vaccines is expected to exacerbate the persistently low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies. If pandemic control falls short of expectations, social distancing and other restrictions may need to be extended in various regions, further undermining the global recovery outlook. Figure 2.3: Share of the population in selected economies that has received at least one dose of a vaccine (as of March 15, 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is underpinned by sustained monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly a monetary policy stance characterized by "lower-for-longer" interest rates. However, there is a risk that the withdrawal of support measures could outpace expectations. For instance, amid the confluence of supply bottlenecks, strong currencies and expanding liquidity, as well as proactive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have risen (Figure 2.4). If future inflation proves stronger than expected, the central bank may need to scale back the magnitude of its monetary easing, while inflation data exceeding forecasts could also lead to increased volatility in financial markets. Figure 2.4: Five-Year Breakeven Inflation Swap Rates in the United States and the Eurozone. Third, significant uncertainty remains in future China–U.S. relations. The trend of US-China "decoupling," particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the onset of the pandemic. Given that both the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States are adopting an increasingly hardline stance toward mainland China, this trend is unlikely to reverse under the Biden administration. If the China-U.S. situation unexpectedly escalates, it could trigger volatility in financial markets in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. Although withdrawing relevant measures prematurely could jeopardize economic recovery and trigger a "cliff effect," in the long run, the costs of maintaining them are substantial. These include imposing fiscal burdens and delaying the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources, such as allowing "zombie enterprises" whose business models are no longer viable to survive on continued government support. Furthermore, policymakers must also address the numerous issues left in the wake of the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending (Figure 2.5). Although the sharp rise in debt is not immediately pressing given that global interest rates are currently at historically low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in both the public and private sectors could fuel concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5: Global debt as a share of gross domestic product. Another unresolved issue concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting trauma that the pandemic may have caused. For instance, heightened uncertainty may prompt firms to reduce investment, while workers who have long struggled with unemployment may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth plummeted in the second quarter of 2020 but stabilized during the second half of the year (Figure 2.6). The momentum for economic recovery is primarily driven by a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand coming from electronics and technical equipment. At the same time, the service sectors most severely hit—such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face interaction with customers—continue to face significant challenges. Figure 2.6: East Asia: Real GDP Growth in 2020. Despite lingering uncertainties in the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have resumed inflows. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted greater bond fund inflows, driven by improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies (Figure 2.7). Amid signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccine production plans, equity fund inflows into East Asia accelerated in the fourth quarter of 2020. Inflows of securities capital also drove appreciation of regional currencies, prompting the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Currency Index to rebound approximately 10% from its low in March of last year. Figure 2.7: East Asia: Cross-border Equity Investment Flows. The East Asia region continues to face ongoing uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines has offered hope to the region's severely affected service sectors and economy, global competition for early vaccine batches has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution has posed challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. Consequently, slower-growing economies within the region may achieve herd immunity later than more advanced ones, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong lockdown measures and delay the recovery of tourism-related sectors. Secondly, since investor optimism is largely driven by vaccine rollout, any significant shortfall in the pace or effectiveness of vaccination could bring the current wave of capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices to an end. A sharp decline in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the successful control of the novel coronavirus and a gradual recovery in consumer activity, China's mainland economy experienced a rapid rebound in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports continued to grow, bolstered by strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech goods) (Figure 2.8). Looking back at 2020, despite the unprecedented economic impact of the novel coronavirus pandemic, mainland China's GDP still recorded a 2.3% growth. Figure 2.8: Mainland China – Contributions of the Components of Demand to GDP Growth. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow robustly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the primary driver of economic expansion. However, whether the economy can sustain its recovery will, to a certain extent, still depend on the trajectory of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities on the mainland have normalized, the service sector continues to face partial disruptions due to the resurgence of the epidemic in several northern provinces. In terms of the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to a fresh wave of the pandemic in most developed economies. Furthermore, the deteriorating Sino-US relationship is unlikely to ease in the short term. However, the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the concluded Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the European Union (CAI) will facilitate China's deeper integration with other economies, potentially offsetting some of the adverse effects of Sino-US decoupling on economic recovery. Given that economic prospects remain uncertain, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that existing policy stances would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasizing the importance of managing systemic risks, such as maintaining macroeconomic leverage stability and ensuring the sustainability of local government debt. Furthermore, the latest government work report has set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the long term, the 14th Five-Year Plan has established technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy as priority development directions, aiming to raise per capita GDP to the level of a moderately developed country by 2035. The impact of the novel coronavirus outbreak on the repayment capacity of issuing companies appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in mainland China's bond market remaining at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp rise in defaults on bonds issued by state-owned enterprises, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Figure 2.9). Although the rise in defaults among state-owned enterprises primarily reflects the central government's resolve to break the "rigid redemption" norm and promote more rational market risk pricing, constrained fiscal space at the local government level—particularly in less developed regions—may also be a contributing factor. Figure 2.9: Mainland China: Size and Proportion of Onshore Bond Defaults. In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and the gradual normalization of interest rates have, to some extent, driven up financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the fourth quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10: Corporate Bond Yields with Five-Year Maturities in Mainland China. In the real estate sector, housing prices in mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, house prices in lower-tier cities have risen much more slowly (Figure 2.11). The oversupply of housing in lower-tier cities, which had been a concern in previous years, was largely brought under control by 2020, partly due to robust sales in these cities amid a surge in market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio for third-tier cities stood at around 13 months, significantly lower than the peak of 31 months recorded in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained significantly below pre-pandemic levels, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as local demand recovered and goods exports expanded further. Amid optimism that vaccination against the novel coronavirus will restore normal economic activity, Hong Kong's economy, which contracted more severely than at any time on record in 2020, is expected to resume growth in 2021. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and efficacy of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, Hong Kong's economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. Accordingly, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures are likely to remain mild. Hong Kong's economy showed some improvement in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained far below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real gross domestic product (GDP) narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further narrowed to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, in 2020, the combined real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 6.1%, marking the largest decline on record and, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019, the first instance of two consecutive years of GDP decline in history. Latest data on value added by industry further indicate that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors contracted year-on-year over recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors experiencing a sharper decline than the overall economy. On a quarterly basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, halting the five consecutive quarters of decline that had preceded it (Table 3.A and Figure 3.1). Local private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, amid the third and fourth waves of local outbreaks, the authorities reimposed social distancing measures, and consumer confidence remained weak. As the business climate briefly improved, overall investment expenditure also increased in the second half of the year. Driven partly by stronger export performance, particularly to the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong's goods trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). Due to the ongoing stagnation in the global tourism sector, trade in services remains weak. Overall, net imports (a trade deficit) weighed on gross domestic product in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower rebound in goods exports compared with imports. Figure 3.1: Growth Rate of Real Gross Domestic Product and Contributions from Major Expenditure Components; Figure 3.2: Real Exports and Imports. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds—the third and fourth—of the Pandemic Prevention and Control Fund between September and December 2020, totaling HK$30.4 billion, to assist sectors and residents affected by the outbreak and to enhance Hong Kong's pandemic preparedness and response capabilities. The Government has also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to stimulate the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of 100% guaranteed special personal loans for unemployed persons. In March 2021, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), in collaboration with the Banking Industry SME Loan Coordination Mechanism, announced the extension of the "Interest-Only, Principal-Deferred" scheme until October of the same year, and also extended the repayment periods for trade finance loans under the scheme. These deferral measures are expected to help alleviate working capital difficulties faced by some corporate clients. The COVID-19 vaccine is expected to help restore normal economic activity, with Hong Kong's economy projected to return to positive growth in 2021 on a full-year basis. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be influenced by numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic, the rollout schedule of vaccines, and their effectiveness. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, Mainland China's economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services. Meanwhile, the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, which in turn will affect Hong Kong's goods trade and inbound tourism. The government forecasts real GDP growth for the full year 2021 to be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts stands at 4.4%. Labor market conditions further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, marking the highest level in 17 years (Figure 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment numbers stabilized after declining to a low point (Figure 3.3), while government figures indicate a continued decline in the number of job vacancies. The Nominal Average Wage Index for employed persons, which reflects labor income, decelerated to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, marking the lowest growth rate in nearly 11 years. To address the persistently deteriorating labour market, the Government launched the "Employment Support Scheme" under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain their staff. Following the conclusion of the "Protect Jobs" scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Epidemic Prevention and Control Fund (such as one-off grants) to further support industries severely impacted by the pandemic. In the short term, given the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Topic 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and decline of Hong Kong's tourism industry on the local labor market. Figure 3.3: Labor Market Conditions  Figure 3.4: Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The core consumer price inflation rate fell sharply on an annual basis to 0.3% in the third quarter and 0.2% in the fourth quarter of 2020, and further declined to -0.5% in January and -0.1% in February 2021 (Figure 3.4). The underlying inflation rate, measured on an annualized basis over the past three months as an indicator of inflationary momentum, has shown only minor fluctuations in recent months while remaining at a low level. Specifically, price pressures on basic foodstuffs have eased, while the cost of dining out has declined noticeably, reflecting that more restaurants have offered takeout promotions during periods when dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures for other traded goods (such as durable goods) remain moderate. In the services sector, with the stabilization of private residential rents, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remains weak (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressures have also moderated in recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.5: Composite Consumer Price Index (Rent Component) and Market Rents. Figure 3.6: Unit Labor Costs. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain moderate in the near term. In particular, with the moderation in rental growth for newly signed private residential leases, domestic inflation will continue to be contained. Market consensus forecasts an overall inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, while the government projects a core inflation rate of 1% and an overall inflation rate of 1.6% for the same year. As the novel coronavirus pandemic raged, Hong Kong's visitor industry plunged into a sharp downturn, sparking market concerns that the crisis would inflict lasting trauma on the recovery of the labor market. Accordingly, this study conducts an empirical analysis of the impact of a thriving tourism sector on Hong Kong's labor market, thereby exploring the potential implications of the current downturn in tourism. Since 2000, Hong Kong's tourism industry has experienced significant fluctuations (Figure B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitors to Hong Kong declined during the 2003 SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak. Since the introduction of the Individual Visit Scheme (independent travel) in July of that year, the number of tourists began to surge. Under the original individual visit scheme, mainland residents could apply to visit Hong Kong once or twice annually in their individual capacity, with each stay not exceeding seven days. Since April 2009, the independent travel program has been expanded to allow qualified Shenzhen residents with local household registration (hukou) to apply for a "Individual Visit" visa permitting multiple entries to Hong Kong within a one-year period (one entry, multiple exits). Since then, the number of mainland tourists has increased significantly. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure projects connecting to mainland China, the number of visitor arrivals in Hong Kong reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events in the latter half of 2019 led to a 50% decline in tourist arrivals, and under the novel coronavirus pandemic, Hong Kong's tourism industry has remained stagnant since late January 2020. Figure B2.1: Tourist Arrivals and Related Policies. Using the growth in the tourism sector driven by the Individual Visit Scheme as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the Individual Visit Scheme introduced in 2003 to be akin to a stochastic economic shock, as its timing was nearly exogenous and unforeseeable to local residents. Our primary analytical data were drawn from population statistics in the Hong Kong Census or the Mid-year Population Census. Specifically, we utilize the 5% samples from the censuses or mid-year population statistics conducted in 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016. In addition, we define the tourism-related sector as comprising the food and beverage, retail, hotel, and transportation industries. First, we employ the difference-in-differences (DiD) analytical framework to compare employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between the treatment group—young workers aged 20 to 40—and the control group—older workers aged 41 to 65. We classified the younger group as the "treatment group" because, being in the early stages of their careers, they are better positioned to make significant adjustments to their employment decisions in response to exogenous growth in Hong Kong's tourism sector. Given that the impact of the tourism boom generated by the Independent Visit Scheme on the labor market may evolve over time, we also employ an event study approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings indicate that, compared with older cohorts, younger workers—particularly women and those with only secondary education—are more likely to enter the tourism-related sector following the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme. Among these, the impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the probability of young women entering tourism-related occupations is particularly pronounced and sustained, remaining at approximately five percentage points higher than the average entry probability of older age groups since 2006 (Figure B2.2). We also employed a similar approach to compare the incomes of those working in the tourism-related sector (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related sectors (control group). Estimates indicate that, following the implementation of the Independent Visit Scheme, workers in tourism-related industries experienced greater income growth than employees in non-tourism sectors. Furthermore, compared with employees in other sectors, women and workers with lower educational attainment in the tourism-related industry have experienced higher income growth, with an upward trend ranging from 3 to 20 percentage points (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2: Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on Female Employment  Figure B2.3: Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on Income for Women and Low-Education Workers  These findings are broadly consistent with international experience, indicating that the tourism sector is a significant source of employment, particularly for young people, women, and workers with lower educational attainment. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are consistent with prior analyses: the robust growth in inbound tourism has increased demand for low-skilled labor, thereby enhancing the resilience of the low-skilled labor market. As Hong Kong's tourism sector has declined from prosperity to a trough, these labor groups may be even more adversely affected, warranting close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continues to hover near the strong-side convertibility guarantee level, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Robust demand for the Hong Kong dollar has been driven primarily by equity-related capital needs, including strong initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activity and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-HK Stock Connect and Shenzhen-HK Stock Connect schemes. As surplus balances have risen to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong interbank rates have broadly declined. Despite the possibility that uncertainties linked to the evolution of the novel coronavirus pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions in China–US relations could intensify capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand the pressures arising from such fluctuations. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has approached the strong-side convertibility guarantee level, driven primarily by equity-related capital demand, including robust new share issuance activity and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Figure 4.1). Although some proceeds from recent initial public offerings were transferred offshore, the Hong Kong stock market sentiment strengthened, and expectations of rising capital demand toward the end of the year supported the Hong Kong dollar, which traded in a narrow range between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December. Amidst continued robust fundraising activity in the first two months of 2021 (see Figure 4.2), the HKD/USD exchange rate closed at 7.7568 on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continue to proceed smoothly and orderly. During the review period, the Strong Side Exchange Rate Guarantee was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the net balance, which reflects substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the Strong Exchange Fund (SEF) was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the linked exchange rate system, the Exchange Fund sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, raising the aggregate balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion by the end of February (Figure 4.3). The Strong Side Conversion Facility was triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicates no signs of significant capital outflow from Hong Kong's banking system. At the same time, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any abnormal capital movements. Figure 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Figure 4.2: Equity capital raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX); Figure 4.3: Summary of balances and Exchange Fund Notes and Bonds. During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar generally declined in line with the depreciation of the US dollar against major currencies (Figure 4.4). Given the narrow inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which has had a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate (REER) index, the trajectory of the REER index has largely mirrored that of the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) index. Figure 4.4 Outlook for Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. Future developments in the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing tensions in China–US relations introduce uncertainties that could exacerbate volatility in capital flows. As an international financial center, Hong Kong hosts a wide range of fundraising activities (such as new share issuances), resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to channel funds into Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be diverted from Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand fluctuations in capital flows without compromising financial stability. Amid continued capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). By component analysis, the increase in the monetary base during this period reflects the rise in the aggregate balance resulting from multiple triggers of the strong-side exchange rate guarantee. On the other hand, other components, including certificates of indebtedness, government-issued currency and coinage, as well as outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds, have remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5: Composition of the Monetary Base. During the review period, large-scale initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar (HKD) deposits arising from IPO subscription loans. Consequently, broad HKD money supply (HKD M3) and its HKD deposit component rose significantly between July and October 2020, as well as in January 2021 (Figure 4.6). As new share fundraising activities concluded and customers repaid their subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, M3 in the Hong Kong dollar increased substantially once again, primarily driven by major new share issuance activities at the end of the month. Overall, over the seven-month period since late June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%. Excluding the impact of share issuance activities in late January, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased moderately by 9.1%. According to the analysis based on corresponding assets, excluding new share subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was primarily driven by an increase in the monetary base triggered by the activation of the strong-side exchange rate guarantee (Figure 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% year-on-year; excluding the impact of the new share issuance at the end of January, they increased moderately by 9.1%. Although term deposit balances in Hong Kong dollars declined due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, which were partly driven by investment needs. Figure 4.6: Deposits of authorized institutions by currency; Figure 4.7: Changes in HKD M3 and corresponding assets. Overall foreign currency deposits have grown steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since the end of June. USD deposits declined slightly by 0.3%, partly reflecting weakness in the US dollar, while deposits in other foreign currencies surged by 15.5% over the same period, primarily driven by an increase in RMB deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits triggered by new share issuance activities, the total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Figure 4.6). Excluding the new share capital raised at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that, as monthly monetary statistics may be subject to short-term factors—such as seasonal fluctuations, capital requirements related to public offerings, and business and investment activities—and consequently exhibit volatility, care should be taken in interpreting these figures. As surpluses have grown, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained at an exceptionally low level throughout the review period (Figure 4.8). Although there was a significant wave of new share fundraising in the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's interbank lending rates remained relatively stable, owing to ample liquidity within the banking system. Overall, Hong Kong's interbank market continues to function normally. Figure 4.8: The HKD USD Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) yield curve generally followed the trajectory of the USD yield curve during the review period, steepening as short-term bond yields declined while long-term bond yields rose (see Figure 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on three-year Hong Kong government bonds declined slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on ten-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Figure 4.9: Government bond yields, composite rates, and average mortgage loan rates at the retail level. Hong Kong dollar (HKD) interest rates at the retail level have primarily declined in tandem with the fall in the HKD interbank offered rate. The composite interest rate reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banking further declined from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% by the end of February 2021 (Figure 4.9). Due to lower funding costs, the average mortgage interest rate for new loans declined from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the trend of the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR). On the other hand, the prime lending rates offered by retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the linked exchange rate system, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate is influenced by U.S. interest rates. Given the persistently low level of US interest rates over the long term, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital market activity and seasonal liquidity demands. Amid highly uncertain macro-financial conditions, the ample liquidity in Hong Kong's banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) have strengthened against the US dollar since late May (Figure 4.10), broadly reflecting China's more favorable economic outlook compared with the rest of the world and a weaker US dollar. In late September, FTSE Russell announced the inclusion of China's onshore government bonds in the World Government Bond Index, further bolstering demand for investment and supporting the appreciation of the renminbi. Throughout most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore rate, with an average premium of approximately 100 basis points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Figure 4.10: Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates. During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (CNH HIBOR) experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demands and seasonal liquidity needs near year-end, it remained below 4% for the majority of the period (Figure 4.11). The three-month offshore Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate for the Renminbi followed the onshore Renminbi interest rate, declining in late December before rising again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Figure 4.11: Overnight and 3-month Offshore RMB Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) Pricing, Second Half of 2020. In the second half of 2020, the offshore RMB liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to expand. Since the fourth quarter, the growth rate of RMB-denominated deposits has accelerated, reflecting in part the appreciation of the renminbi and its relatively higher interest rates compared to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the balance of RMB-denominated customer deposits and certificates of deposit accelerated in growth, reaching RMB 826.3 billion by the end of January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Figure 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits increased by 24.7%, primarily driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, the balance of deposit certificates decreased by 25.0% year-on-year. Figure 4.12: RMB deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. With regard to other RMB business, over the seven-month period from the end of June 2020, the outstanding balance of RMB loans declined by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion. On the other hand, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow robustly. From July 2020 to January 2021, Hong Kong banks processed RMB 3.7695 trillion in transactions, a 16.7% increase compared to the same period last year. In the relevant transactions, the increase in remittances transferred from Hong Kong to mainland China was greater than the increase in remittances sent from the mainland to Hong Kong (Figure 4.13). Hong Kong possesses a substantial RMB liquidity pool, sufficient to continue supporting extensive RMB payments and financial transactions. In 2020, the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system recorded a daily average transaction volume of RMB 1.1915 trillion, up from RMB 1.1339 trillion in 2019.

Amidst the recurring COVID-19 pandemic, which has prolonged economic downturns, and in the context of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong's retail banks saw their profitability decline further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remains sound, given its robust capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, to continue supporting the broader economy in navigating these challenges, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong decided to extend a number of relief measures. Looking ahead, while the rollout of vaccines may fuel hopes for global pandemic control and the resumption of economic activity, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties and persistent geopolitical tensions are adverse to business activity and continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may erode the repayment capacity of enterprises and households; therefore, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of these downside risk factors on asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the retail banking division's pre-tax operating profit declined by 38.5% compared to the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared to 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.1). The net interest margin for retail banking narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.2), reducing net interest income and outweighing the modest growth in non-interest income, thereby leading to a decline in profitability. For the full year 2020, the retail banking segment's overall pre-tax operating profit declined by 29.4%, while return on assets fell from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Figure 5.1: Profitability of Retail Banking. Figure 5.2: Net Interest Margin of Retail Banking. The net interest margin of retail banking has generally been under pressure due to abundant liquidity in the Hong Kong dollar, driven by substantial capital inflows into the stock market. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Among these, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) declined by 43 basis points in the second half of the year, reaching 0.35% by the end of 2020 (blue line in Figure 5.3). The trend of the composite interest rate—a metric measuring the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks—was broadly similar, falling sharply from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% by the end of 2020 (green line in Figure 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflects a decrease in interbank funding costs and rate cuts on fixed deposit rates by certain major retail banks. Figure 5.3. From a broader perspective, the average overall funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars for licensed banks declined moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4: Funding Costs and Maturity Outlook for HKD and USD of Licensed Banks. Looking ahead, given that the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to pressure banks' net interest margins, the profitability outlook for the banking sector remains challenging. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have bolstered market optimism regarding global economic prospects, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the significant uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. The aforementioned risk factors will continue to affect the credit quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capital adequacy of Hong Kong's banking sector remains robust, substantially exceeding the minimum international standards. As of end-December 2020, the combined total capital ratio of locally registered authorized institutions stood at 20.7%, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Figure 5.5). The novel coronavirus outbreak dealt a severe shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market volatility, some open-ended funds experienced substantial net outflows (Figure B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Figure B1.1: Outflows from select open-ended funds during the March 2020 events. In addition to investors' liquidity needs, a further driver of substantial outflows may have been investors' adoption of a first-mover advantage to redeem early, thereby avoiding potentially sharp increases in redemption costs under stressed market conditions. To curb capital outflows triggered by first-mover advantage, certain open-ended funds employ swing pricing—a pricing mechanism for open-ended funds that mitigates the first-mover advantage for investors. Although many open-ended funds employed swing pricing during this event, no empirical research has demonstrated whether swing pricing effectively reduces outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this study conducts empirical research to examine whether swing pricing during the March 2020 events could have mitigated outflows from open-ended funds, thereby reducing their liquidity risk. Additionally, this study will identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we will formulate policy recommendations to safeguard financial stability. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming their holdings before others, thereby shifting the redemption costs onto the remaining investors. First-mover advantages are primarily observed in open-end funds that adhere to traditional pricing rules, whereby the subscription and redemption costs incurred by fund investors (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the fund's price only after the transaction is executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This serves as an incentive for early redemption, particularly in anticipation of substantial redemption costs. Consequently, under market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to the expectation of rising redemption costs. This has intensified redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-end funds.

Amidst heightened risk-aversion in the local equity market and concerns over the normalization of U.S. monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. With ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) continue to remain at low levels. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continues to proceed smoothly and orderly. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions could amplify volatility in capital flows, Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system equip it to withstand the shocks associated with such fluctuations. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar has remained predominantly within the strong side of the exchange rate band, and trading has continued to proceed smoothly and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid heightened risk-aversion sentiment in the local stock market (Figure 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar staged a modest rebound in October 2021 amid improved market sentiment, its upward momentum subsequently faded, primarily due to weak net southbound inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Figure 4.2) and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, new share fundraising activities continued to support the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately over the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. At the same time, the latest balance of payments figures show that foreign direct investment from non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of abnormal cross-border capital movements. Figure 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Figure 4.2: Net southbound purchases via the Shanghai-HK Connect and Shenzhen-HK Connect; Figure 4.3: Equity capital raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX). Despite the strengthening of the US dollar over the review period, the Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable, supported by the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Figure 4.4). Given the narrow inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate index has largely tracked the movements of its nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.4 Outlook for nominal and real effective exchange rates: Uncertainties surrounding U.S. monetary policy, the evolution of the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate volatility in capital flows. As US interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar liquidity—whose pace and magnitude will depend on prevailing market conditions at the time—could weaken the HKD and trigger the Weak-side Convertibility Guarantee. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow fluctuations without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base rose by 1.4% over the eight months following the end of June 2021, primarily driven by an increase in the issuance of liability certificates. This reflects an increase in outstanding Exchange Fund Notes (EFNs) driven by sustained demand for EFNs from the banking system amid ample liquidity, which in turn reduced the summary balance (prior to discount window operations) by HK$119.9 billion to HK$3,376 billion. During the review period, the combined outstanding amount of EFNs and bonds rose by HK$119.7 billion to HK$11,887 billion (Figure 4.5). At the same time, paper currency and coins issued by the government have remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5 summarizes that over the six-month period since the end of July 2021, total deposits held by authorized institutions increased moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal patterns, fundraising requirements related to public offerings, and business and investment activities; therefore, it is advisable to examine longer-term trends. In 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. Figure 4.6: Total deposits of authorized institutions by currency. Overall, Hong Kong's interbank market continues to operate smoothly and orderly. Amid robust liquidity in the banking system, Hong Kong's interbank offered rates have remained low despite market concerns over tightening U.S. monetary policy (Figure 4.7). Some indications suggest that market expectations point to a rise in funding demand toward year-end, leading to a slight increase in Hong Kong interbank offered rates in December 2021. The average interest rate on newly originated mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of the major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, the banking system enjoys ample liquidity and will be able to provide a robust buffer in the event of major capital market activities or financial market volatility. Figure 4.7: Review of Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates. During the review period, the offshore RMB interbank market continued to operate normally. Influenced by seasonal liquidity demand near the year-end, the overnight Hong Kong offshore Renminbi (CNH) interbank offered rate experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH interbank offered rate remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Figure 4.8). Figure 4.8: Overnight and 3-month Offshore RMB Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) Pricing, Second Half of 2021. During the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months from the end of July 2021, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1.1135 trillion as of the end of January 2022 (Figure 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits rose by 33.5%, primarily driven by corporate fund inflows, which offset a 48.0% decline in the outstanding balance of certificates of deposit. Figure 4.9: Hong Kong's RMB deposits and deposit certificates. Over the six-month period since July 2021, although the outstanding balance of RMB loans declined by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. From late July 2021 to late January 2022, banks in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region processed transactions totaling RMB 3.763 trillion, an 18.3% increase compared to RMB 3.181 trillion in the same period of the previous year (Figure 4.10). Hong Kong's substantial renminbi liquidity pool continues to support a wide range of renminbi payment and financing transactions. In 2021, the average daily transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system rose from RMB 1.1915 trillion in 2020 to RMB 1.5226 trillion. Figure 4.10 Outlook for RMB Trade Settlement and Remittance. In the future, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the north–south Stock Connect, Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of China's capital account, growing demand from international investors for RMB-denominated assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Greater Bay Area framework. Global major equity indices continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but amid growing concerns over the tightening stances of major central banks in developed economies and escalating tensions between Russia and Ukraine, they have since consolidated from January 2022. The Hong Kong equity market remained sluggish throughout the fourth quarter of 2021, primarily weighed down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and the uncertainty surrounding the development of Hong Kong's epidemic pushed the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low in late February. At the same time, the offshore RMB bond market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly due to a weakening sentiment in the asset markets and a new wave of local outbreaks. Global equity markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, propelling the Morgan Stanley Capital International World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Figure 4.11). Driven by government monetary and fiscal stimulus, the global economic recovery and robust corporate earnings have underpinned the upward trend in major global stock markets, though the pandemic remains investors' primary concern throughout the year. However, major global equity markets have begun to consolidate since early January 2022, amid growing concerns over the tightening stances of central banks in developed economies in response to sharply rising inflation risks, a surge in commodity prices, and escalating tensions from the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, by the end of 2021, Hong Kong's equity market continued to lag behind other major global stock markets. The Hang Seng Index traded between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September through mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, a 14.1% decline from 2020. In early 2022, renewed interest from value investors in Hong Kong equities helped push the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, the uncertainty surrounding Hong Kong's evolving pandemic situation, compounded by the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict, dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a two-year low of 22,713 points by the end of February. Over the entire review period from late August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index declined by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Figure 4.11). Figure 4.11: The Hang Seng Index and the Morgan Stanley Capital International World Index. Due to the highly transmissible Omicron variant, implied volatility in equity markets surged in late November 2021 before subsequently subsiding. Although the skew index has retreated from its historic high in late June 2021, it remains elevated, reflecting investor concerns that the stock market's sustained rally since the onset of the pandemic may face a correction. Consequently, investors are willing to allocate additional capital to hedge against potential equity downside risks (Figure 4.12). Figure 4.12: Options-implied volatility and skew indices for the Hang Seng Index and the S&P 500. Amid globally ample liquidity conditions, the Hong Kong equity market has continued to record net capital inflows from international investors since the last report (Figure 4.13). In contrast, the Southbound channel of the Stock Connect experienced significant net capital outflows in the third quarter of 2021, primarily driven by concerns over the impact of mainland regulatory changes on technology stocks. However, buying flows through the Stock Connect southbound channel began to recover in December 2021, recording a net inflow of HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, net fund inflows rose cumulatively by 5.7% to HK$22,330 billion (Figure 4.14). The easing of mainland China's monetary policy, coupled with an increasing number of Chinese companies listing in Hong Kong's primary market via secondary listings, is expected to boost sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market continues to face numerous headwinds, including uncertainty over the local pandemic trajectory, a faster-than-expected normalization of US monetary policy, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Hong Kong retail banks saw their profits decline in the second half of 2021. The ratio of classified loans rose slightly in the second half of 2021, yet remains at a low level when measured against both historical and international benchmarks. Amidst sound capital and liquidity conditions, Hong Kong's banking sector remains robust. During the review period, to further assist the economy in navigating the difficult times, the Monetary Authority continued to implement a range of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to economic recovery, while the risk of the Federal Reserve normalizing monetary policy at a pace faster than anticipated will jointly challenge banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the retail banking division's pre-tax operating profit declined by 16.1% compared to the same period in 2020. Weak earnings performance was primarily driven by declines in net interest and non-interest income, alongside an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, down from 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.1). For the full year 2021, the retail banking division's total pre-tax operating profit decreased by 18.6% year-on-year compared to 2020, while return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Figure 5.1 illustrates how sustained low-interest rates have impacted retail bank profitability, with net interest margins remaining at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2: The net interest margin of retail banks reflects year-end funding requirements and the decline in the outstanding balance of Exchange Fund Bills following their issuance, resulting in a slight increase in the Hong Kong interbank offered rate (HIBOR) in the fourth quarter of 2021. However, given that liquidity in the banking system remains ample, interbank interest rates continue to remain at relatively low levels. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose modestly by 9 basis points over the preceding six months, reaching 0.26% by the end of December 2021 (see the blue line in Figure 5.3). The cost of funds for the retail banking segment remained stable during the review period. The composite interest rate, an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banking, rose modestly by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months ago to 0.21% by the end of 2021 (green line in Figure 5.3). The overall cost of funds has been calculated as a weighted average based on the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with those from prior months. Although the normalization of U.S. monetary policy may signal an improvement in bank profitability, near-term gains could be partially offset by two factors. First, although the Federal Reserve has indicated that it will raise interest rates multiple times in 2022, past experience suggests that local interest rate adjustments may lag behind US rate movements, particularly when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains ample. Therefore, the improvement in banks' net interest margins may take longer to materialize. Furthermore, the surge in Omicron variant cases may introduce uncertainties into the pace of economic recovery, thereby placing pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. In this regard, the HKMA has dedicated substantial resources to advancing Hong Kong's climate objectives and contributing to the enhancement of global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's integration of our inaugural Sustainability Report as a chapter within the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's 2021 Annual Report, we have, for the first time this year, published our 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document. This report aims to provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategic priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking sector's capacity to address climate change, fostering a green finance ecosystem, and advancing its role as a responsible investor and institution committed to sustainable development. This year, we have made significant progress in advancing sustainable development across the major functions of the Monetary Authority. Readers will find in this report our concrete measures and work, with key focus areas including the fact that banks' daily operations face climate-related risks. As the banking regulator, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has taken concrete measures to enhance banks' capacity to address climate change. In 2022, we established a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into regulatory procedures and to explore how technology can assist banks in assessing the impacts of physical risks. Recognizing the growing proliferation of green and sustainable products by banks, we have shared industry best practices on their effective management to enhance banks' capacity for climate risk management. The Monetary Authority of Singapore actively participates in various collaborative initiatives aimed at addressing climate risks and advancing the development of sustainable finance. At the local level, we are collaborating with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Coordinating Group (the Coordinating Group) to develop a local green taxonomy. This framework will enhance transparency in financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively engaging with multiple international organizations to help formulate climate change policies and assess their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet the demand for green and sustainable financing in Asia. Despite 2022 being a particularly challenging year for the global bond market, Hong Kong continued to record robust growth in green and sustainable debt issuance, with a 42% increase to a total of USD 80.5 billion, cementing its position as the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances.² Relevant issuers include the People's Governments of Shenzhen Municipality and Hainan Province.
