Their bond issuances further underscore Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the mainland and the international community. The robust growth of Hong Kong's green bond market can be attributed in part to the government's Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the Monetary Authority has assisted the government in issuing green bonds totaling nearly US$16 billion. The proceeds have been allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts," including in May 2022, when we helped issue the first tranche of government green retail bonds totaling HK$20 billion, which at the time represented the largest green retail bond issuance globally. Additionally, we assisted the government in issuing the first batch of tokenized green bonds in February 2023. This marks the world's first government-issued tokenized green bond, and the issuance represents a milestone in our successful integration of strengths across the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, which can only be established through the efforts and collaboration of diverse sectors. To this end, the HKMA primarily advances these elements through its Steering Group, collaborating with other relevant government departments, regulatory bodies, academic institutions, and the financial industry. In addition to the development of a local green taxonomy framework as previously discussed, the Steering Committee has also promoted industry skills training and enhanced Hong Kong's data resources through its established Green and Sustainable Finance Centre. In addition, the Oversight Group has made solid progress in other areas, including mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and opportunities in carbon markets. In 2022, the Exchange Fund further strengthened its efforts in responsible investing, notably setting a target for its investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we have also enhanced our risk management framework to strengthen the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and improve its risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capitalize on the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to advancing the sustainable investment of the Exchange Fund by identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the long-term returns of our portfolio. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to 2017 levels. In fact, the Exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets remains consistently lower than that of the overall market. Moving forward, we will continue our journey toward net-zero emissions by systematically integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into our investment management processes, actively exercising our ownership rights, maintaining ongoing collaboration with all stakeholders, and focusing on decarbonization and transition within our investment portfolios. At the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Committee on Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the Authority's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: environmental stewardship, employee well-being, and social responsibility. In terms of the environment, we are committed to fostering a green workplace and promoting more environmentally friendly markets to society. Regarding our employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively cultivate a healthy and inclusive work environment. In the realm of social responsibility, we strive to enhance the public's financial literacy, advance financial inclusion, and actively give back to society. Compared to our 2015 baseline for tracking carbon footprint, we achieved double-digit reductions in per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage by 2022. More importantly, we have established a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained, multi-stakeholder efforts and collaboration. On this critical global issue, we recognize the imperative to lead by example and work collaboratively with like-minded industry peers and international organizations. In the next section, we will outline the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's short-term plans and key priorities in addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is a formidable challenge, and we are committed to doing everything in our power to meet this goal. We are confident that, with the joint efforts of all colleagues, the financial industry, and the general public, we will successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. President, Yu Weiwen.

In 2023, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will continue to advance sustainable development within Hong Kong's financial sector and uphold its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainability-focused institution. At the same time, by participating in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking sector regulator, we are committed to strengthening the industry's climate resilience, further enhancing our green finance ecosystem, and supporting banks' green transformation. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to assess their progress in implementing regulatory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review processes, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector's "green benchmark." At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example by exploring various measures and technical solutions to assist banks in identifying, quantifying, and monitoring their climate risk exposures. The Monetary Authority of Singapore will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing, as part of the regulator-led periodic stress testing cycle for the 2023–2024 period. Participating banks will be required to assess their capacity to manage climate-related risks using an optimized stress-testing framework that incorporates a range of stress scenarios, including extreme weather events and adverse economic conditions. To foster the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will closely monitor local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain ongoing dialogue with the industry, and issue timely guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to comprehensively evaluate the green and sustainable investment products offered by the bank. At the same time, to strengthen the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector's green transition, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green taxonomy framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will assist the Government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the programme's scope to include sustainable development bonds. At the same time, the Authority will attract more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA also assists in implementing the government-funded Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. In addition, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will continue to encourage more mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to access green financing through Hong Kong, and will explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with financial technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other agencies and departments through the Cross-sectoral Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance on cross-industry issues, including skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as opportunities in the carbon market. Through the Green Banking Alliance, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will jointly launch a series of targeted initiatives with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) across Asia. These include conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering tailored professional training for banks, and delivering practical guidelines to assist banks in developing roadmaps to integrate green finance into their core business strategies. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership program aimed at expanding the Alliance's influence across Asia. At the same time, the Alliance will strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of knowledge on green finance, and lead the development of new project initiatives. As a responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has set a target to achieve net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund portfolio by 2050 or earlier, in line with its commitment to contribute to global climate action and to implement the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). Looking ahead, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong will continue to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into its investment management processes, strive toward net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable institution, the Monetary Authority is committed not only to the well-being of its employees but also to the broader community and the environment in which it operates. We have established a sustainable development roadmap and set climate targets for our operations as part of our commitment to global decarbonization and climate action. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will continue to prioritize the reduction of carbon emissions and encourage all staff to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction efforts. Furthermore, we will provide additional guidance to employees to integrate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To advance digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will explore approaches to modernize its internal systems and applications. This initiative aims to further improve operational efficiency while minimizing potential risks associated with the digital transformation process.

Climate change represents a significant risk to the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) remains committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face a range of sustainability and climate-related issues in their daily operations. To continue fulfilling their vital role within the financial system and channel more capital toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong has placed particular emphasis on strengthening banks' capacity to address and manage climate risks, while accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and has participated in the recent Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued the Principles for the Effective Management and Supervision of Climate-related Financial Risks and issued responses to frequently asked questions to clarify how the existing Basel framework addresses these risks. In response to these global developments, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue its efforts to integrate climate-related factors into its regulatory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual Module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has continued to engage with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges related to the implementation of the relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen regulatory oversight of banks' climate risk management, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the banking regulatory framework, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the Monetary Authority of Singapore issued an amended Unit SA-1 of the Supervisory Policy Manual, titled "Risk-Based Supervisory Framework," and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by integrating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, the Monetary Authority has refined the climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework, drawing on lessons learned from the 2021 pilot scheme. The HKMA has also formulated a plan to integrate the next round of climate risk stress tests into the regulatory authorities' regular stress testing framework, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year plan, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is also strengthening its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. At the same time, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is reviewing the regulatory review process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy levels and to determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements. This review aims to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks in addressing climate change risks and risks associated with the transition to carbon neutrality. In light of the increasing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) conducted a thematic review, primarily examining banks' development and ongoing management of such products. During its thematic review, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) identified several best practices and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, thereby enabling banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. Application of technology can enhance data availability and strengthen banks' capacity to manage climate risk. The Monetary Authority has begun developing a universal platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on the real estate sector. In addition, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with other central banks and regulatory bodies, has completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements' Innovation Hub to explore how technological solutions can assist in assessing physical risks. The Monetary Authority also places great emphasis on promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices. These efforts leverage advanced analytics and regulatory technology, supported by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has streamlined its anti-money laundering regulatory data collection processes to alleviate the staffing burden on banks and reduce paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and foster greater alignment in green finance policies, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green taxonomy framework. The Green Classification Framework, commonly referred to as the Green Classification Catalogue, categorizes economic activities as either green or sustainable. It serves as a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether a specific activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained close contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to thoroughly examine the framework's characteristics and challenges, and is preparing to propose and consult on the framework's structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. The Monetary Authority recognizes that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system; accordingly, it has expanded the scope of climate-related factors and scenarios incorporated into financial risk analysis and research to strengthen current monitoring efforts. In its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority takes climate change into account and incorporates analyses of climate-related risks into its financial stability reports. By actively participating in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the impacts of climate change on the macroeconomy and the financial system. In terms of research activities, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) carried out several applied research projects in 2022, conducting in-depth investigations into two key topics: greenwashing in the corporate green bond market and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate-related risks. The aforementioned research findings can inform the formulation of policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Locally, these studies will strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with various stakeholders through multiple channels, including international central bank research seminars and the Authority's semi-annual report on Monetary and Financial Stability. The HKMA's Liquidity Facility Framework is a secured standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is exploring the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is actively engaged in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and advancing sustainable finance as a mainstream priority. Through its engagement in this area, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has helped foster international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, while drawing on insights to enhance the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA has intensified efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide essential infrastructure and incentives, and support international initiatives while aligning with global standards. The Cross-sectoral Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group) is jointly led by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). It is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy. The Steering Group's work is primarily based on its strategic plan, which outlines six key focus areas and five action agendas to strengthen Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and build a greener, more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong's position as a global risk management hub. Facilitate the flow of climate-related information across all levels to support risk management, capital allocation, and investor protection. Enhance the skills of industry practitioners and raise public awareness and engagement. Encourage product innovation and research initiatives to channel funds toward green and sustainable projects. Capitalize on opportunities arising from mainland China to develop Hong Kong as the Greater Bay Area's green finance center. Deepen regional and international cooperation. To date, the Steering Group has made significant progress in advancing Hong Kong's sustainable finance agenda since its establishment. The Supervisory Working Group's current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre (see below), the development of a green taxonomy (see "Building a Sustainable Financial System: Establishing a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Capital Flows" on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and opportunities in the carbon market. Specifically, the Steering Committee will publish a preliminary feasibility assessment of opportunities for Hong Kong's carbon market in March and support Hong Kong's development as a regional carbon trading hub, including fostering a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalizing on opportunities arising from Greater Bay Area cooperation. In December, the Oversight Team announced a collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data accessibility in Hong Kong and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, both parties have developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeted at non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This initiative facilitates corporate sustainability reporting while enabling financial institutions to collect and analyze company-level data for risk assessment and related business decision-making. This represents a significant step by the oversight committee in expanding the scope of its data collection to include small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), a vital yet historically difficult-to-reach segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre in July 2021 to coordinate training and policy development efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and academic institutions, and to build relevant resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three databases focusing on data, training information, and internship opportunities to support the financial sector and other industries in accessing green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. The Resource Repository provides data sources to support the assessment of Hong Kong's physical climate risks. To assist in industry talent development, the Centre collaborated with the Government in December to launch the "Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme," which offers financial support to practitioners, students, and graduates participating in training and skills enhancement programs related to green and sustainable finance. Other measures to promote skills training include launching the "Sustainable Finance Internship Programme" to create more internship opportunities for students, and introducing a new Module 3 on "Green and Sustainable Finance" under the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's "Banking Professional Qualifications Framework" for banking practitioners. The Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) launched the Green Commercial Banking Alliance, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry associations, research bodies, and technology innovators to jointly develop a collaborative platform for advancing green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realize their potential, establishing green finance as a mainstream core business, and to foster the financial sector's active participation in global climate change initiatives. The Alliance operates as a one-stop peer learning platform for financial institutions, equipping them with the knowledge, tools, and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions. It brings together green finance leaders, connects green finance institutions across diverse emerging markets to foster dialogue, and addresses cutting-edge issues to advance the global green finance agenda, thereby unlocking a wealth of green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions became founding members of the Alliance. In close collaboration with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the Alliance encourages clients to adopt green strategies, promotes best practices in green products and services, and helps unlock new business opportunities, contributing to the transition toward a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner committed in 2022 to provide climate expertise in areas such as innovation, standardization, and academic research. Details of the alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version). In parallel, since March 2021, the alliance has organized 18 training sessions and roundtable discussions, attracting over 6,000 participants from across the globe, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. Furthermore, in June 2022, the Alliance, in collaboration with the HK Monetary and Financial Research Centre (the Centre), released its inaugural frontier research report titled "Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices, and Regulation." The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been promoting the issuance of green and sustainable debt and fostering a local ecosystem of related professional services. In 2022, the total amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong, including bonds and loans, reached US$80.5 billion, representing a 42% increase. Green and sustainable debt issuance increased by 42%, reaching US$80.5 billion. To demonstrate the Government's resolve in addressing climate change and to advance green finance while fostering Hong Kong's development as a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the Green Bond Financing Programme in 2018, with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority assisting in the implementation of related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued green institutional and retail bonds totaling nearly US$16 billion. The proceeds have been allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the program, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report, which details the allocation of proceeds raised from green bonds and their anticipated environmental benefits. To enable citizens to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development and share in its benefits, the first tranche of green retail bonds totaling HK$20 billion was issued in May. The issuance received a robust response from the public, making it the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance further diversifies the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, reinforcing its position as a leading green finance hub in the region and globally. The Government also continued its regular green bond issuance program in the 2022-23 fiscal year, issuing green bonds equivalent to USD 5.75 billion in January 2023. This issuance of three currencies—US dollars, euros, and renminbi—features maturities ranging from two to 30 years, continuing to provide a critical benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the broader region. The issuance was widely welcomed by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not previously participated in the Government's green bond offerings, underscoring strong investor confidence in Hong Kong's long-term creditworthiness and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the government has doubled the issuance volume of renminbi bonds to 10 billion yuan. The allocation for international investors and for mainland investors participating in this issuance via the Bond Connect "Southbound" channel also increased, underscoring Hong Kong's position as the leading offshore RMB hub and further cementing its leadership role as an international financial centre. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) also assisted the government in issuing tokenized institutional green bonds in February 2023 to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This is among the world's first tokenized green bonds issued by a government. This primary issuance was settled on a private blockchain network using T+1 settlement, with subsequent processes—including coupon payments, secondary market trading settlement, and redemption at maturity—also digitized. The experience gained from this government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond offerings in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region. According to the International Capital Market Association's report, Hong Kong emerged in 2022 as the leading hub in Asia for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds, with a total volume of $27.8 billion, accounting for more than one-third of the region's total. Asia serves as the global hub for international green and sustainable bond issuance, with a total volume of $27.8 billion. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government reissued RMB 5 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB 2.6 billion in green and blue bonds. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People's Government also issued, for the first time, RMB 5 billion in offshore bonds in Hong Kong, including blue bonds and sustainable bonds. These bond issuance activities have repeatedly underscored Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring position as the region's premier fundraising platform. The Monetary Authority of Hong Kong continues to promote and implement the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in 2021, leveraging the initiative to attract more relevant professional service providers—including financial institutions, green advisory firms, and external verifiers—to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The initiative has been widely embraced by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the programme had covered pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both pre- and post-issuance external review services for more than 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments, helping them ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. Since March, the scheme has been optimized by lowering the minimum loan threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, thereby enabling smaller enterprises to access green financing. Following the successful proof-of-concept for tokenized retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Bank for International Settlements' Innovation Hub in Hong Kong have collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digital carbon forwards, also known as Mitigation Outcome Instruments (MOIs). This initiative aims to enhance transparency, objectivity, and environmental integrity within the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that utilize blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver, and transfer digitized MOIs.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) plays a pivotal role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The Monetary Authority is a pioneer in responsible investing. As early as 2015, it led investments in green and sustainable assets, required its external investment managers to adopt the Securities and Futures Commission's Principles of Responsible Ownership, and integrated environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the management of the Exchange Fund's portfolio. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, long-term value growth," and believes that incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value and mitigate associated risks. In response to the increasingly severe climate change challenges, the Exchange Fund has continued its journey toward responsible investment, including setting a "Net Zero by 2050" target in 2022 and refining its risk management strategies. These efforts aim to enhance the resilience of its investment portfolio, thereby securing more favorable risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Fund. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is also actively building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, collaborating with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment, and working with international organizations to establish ESG investment standards. Transparency in climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To uphold its commitment to support the Net-Zero Banking Alliance's Glasgow Declaration, issued by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 UN Climate Change Conference, and to advance the greening of the global financial system, the Monetary Authority has made climate-related disclosures regarding the Exchange Fund in line with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term  b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment  c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System  d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures  The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, has established a framework and guiding principles for responsible investment, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the management of the Exchange Fund's investments. The primary guiding principle is for the Monetary Authority to prioritize ESG investments that deliver risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to other projects, thereby upholding the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the Exchange Fund's Responsible Investment Framework are available on the HKMA website. The Investment Committee, established under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio. The Investment Committee reviews the Responsible Investment Framework and Risk Management Guidelines and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the Exchange Fund's ESG performance through regular reports from the Risk Management and Surveillance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As illustrated in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established within the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and overseeing all ESG-related activities of the Investment Office. The motions discussed and progress updates from each meeting of the ESG Committee will be reported to the Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The dedicated task force of the Risk Management and Oversight Department, in close collaboration with the investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, is responsible for integrating ESG factors and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across various investment portfolios. In relation to public market investments, the Credit, Regulatory and Oversight Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed-income portfolio through regular reporting from the Risk Management and Oversight Department. In addition, the Risk Management and Oversight Department participates in the selection, appointment, and oversight of external investment managers for the equity portfolio from an ESG perspective (see the section "Proactively Exercising Ownership Rights" under "Risk Management" on page 27). In private market investments, the Investment Committee, chaired by the President of the Monetary Authority, will review the ESG-related assessments conducted by the Risk Management and Surveillance Department and the Private Market Investment Team for each investment proposal. Specific evidence² continues to demonstrate that the impacts of climate change and associated risks are significant. According to the latest report of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)³, even if all countries fully implement their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) as pledged, global average temperature is projected to rise by 2.1 to 2.4°C by 2100, making it unlikely that the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels will be achieved. If regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴, coupled with market re-pricing of assets based on anticipated future trends and inherent physical risks, will intensify pressure on asset valuations. In light of updated global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, leveraging the expertise of external consultants, has conducted an additional assessment of the resilience of the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio under a "rapid transition" scenario (Figure 2), building upon the scenario analyses previously carried out in 2021. The "Rapid Transition" scenario incorporates elevated transition risk factors across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons. It assumes that policy changes and technological advancements jointly drive a swift decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets face sudden divestment to keep global average temperature rise below 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100. The scenario aligns broadly with the NGFS's recommended disorderly scenario for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The portfolio is resilient over the medium to long term, owing to the substantial allocation to sovereign bonds that are relatively insensitive to transition risks. Industry distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may adversely impact performance in the short term, particularly for equity assets. The portfolio as a whole will increasingly be impacted by physical risks that gradually materialize over time. The energy and traditional utilities sectors remain the most vulnerable. Climate scenarios, like other modeling approaches, have their limitations. The analysis is based on the benchmark sector allocation at the strategic asset allocation level and does not account for the impact of active security selection within individual sectors. Deeper analysis reveals that, compared with market benchmarks for strategic asset allocation, investments within portfolios generally demonstrate greater resilience to transition-related shocks or suffer less severe impacts. This result once again affirms that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's focus on responsible investing to combat climate change can enhance the resilience of investment portfolios. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve alongside improvements in data quality and policy development. The Exchange Fund will regularly review relevant scenarios and enhance its assessment framework to better evaluate the resilience of the Exchange Fund in the face of climate change. As a long-term investor, the Monetary Authority fully recognizes both the risks and opportunities presented by climate change. The Monetary Authority is committed to further expanding sustainable investments, while capitalizing on opportunities related to climate transition, mitigating climate risks, and enhancing long-term portfolio returns. In 2022, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) sustained its strong momentum, increasing its holdings of green, social, and sustainable bonds by a further 50%. In equity investments, the Monetary Authority maintains an actively managed portfolio focused on corporate governance, while employing a low-carbon strategy for its passive equity portfolio that favors companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is in discussions with the dedicated partners of the Exchange Fund's Long-Term Growth Portfolio to establish a dedicated private equity portfolio aimed at advancing green and sustainable development in Asia (see Figure 3). Figure 3 outlines the ongoing measures to expand ESG investment. The Monetary Authority has invested in a pan-African wind power operator that, in addition to generating clean energy, places strong emphasis on social factors and biodiversity conservation. Before the establishment of the wind farm, local villagers used poisoned baits to deter predators from preying on their livestock, but this practice inadvertently endangered certain vulture species that are classified as threatened. Livestock constitutes a vital asset for local villagers. To assist them in protecting their animals, the wind farm operator has constructed livestock shelters within the wind farm to safeguard the livestock from predation by wild animals. Additionally, operators employ bird-monitoring teams to issue alerts when vultures are drawn to animal carcasses left by predators, triggering the shutdown of wind turbines to prevent collisions with the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win outcome: it safeguards villagers' livelihoods while also minimizing collisions between vultures and wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Robust ESG practices can unlock new business opportunities and diversify revenue streams for enterprises, as illustrated by the following supply chain operations. The investee company is a comprehensive logistics and warehousing operator based in mainland China, specializing in cold chain services for pharmaceuticals, chemical products, and high-end consumer goods. The company faces escalating ESG operational standards, driven primarily by its multinational corporate clients requiring their suppliers to meet high decarbonization targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these requirements, the company engaged external consultants to develop a "Three-Year ESG Plan" aimed at reducing carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonization plan has already delivered significant results as early as 2021. The above ESG measures earned the company the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing. These achievements and accolades have enabled the company to secure significant business opportunities with multinational consumer and chemical product clients that place particular emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investing is inextricably linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The Monetary Authority actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to advance responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong (MAHK) successfully hosted its fourth annual ESG workshop, facilitating exchanges with nine participating private market institutions—including general partners, limited partners, and corporate entities—on best practices in ESG implementation, while promoting sustainable investment opportunities across the Asia-Pacific region and the Greater Bay Area of Guangdong, Hong Kong, and Macao. In the open market, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) urged its counterparties, primarily investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. In his opening remarks at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop, Mr. David Li, Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, highlighted the HKMA's active role at the international level in shaping industry ESG investment standards and practices. As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a joint initiative coordinated by PRI signatories to develop a harmonized responsible investment due diligence questionnaire for private equity and venture capital investments. This initiative aims to assist private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of general partners and investment recommendations. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has participated in several working groups to support FCLTGlobal's research, which aims to examine leading market practices for long-term portfolios and decarbonizing private assets, as well as the applicability of these practices to long-term investors. As a member of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and a supporter of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), the Hong Kong Monetary Authority contributed to the NGFS' Central Bank Climate-related Disclosure Guidelines, demonstrating its commitment to adopting best practices in ESG. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) led a working group under the Network for Greening the Financial System's (NGFS) Central Bank Net Zero Working Group to develop sustainable and responsible investment guidelines for the central banking community. The Monetary Authority continues to actively participate in various industry forums and lectures, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. Liu Huijuan, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (center), addressed the audience at the ESG Investment Opportunities Sharing Session, emphasizing that building internal capabilities is crucial for advancing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to undertake relevant courses on sustainable development and obtain pertinent qualifications, the HKMA has also drawn upon relevant knowledge and practical experience from a 2021 engagement with external consultants who advised on leading industry practices for climate transition within investment portfolios. On the other hand, the Exchange Fund utilizes ESG data compiled by reputable third-party information providers to complement its ongoing portfolio analysis, thereby strengthening the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The Monetary Authority is committed to reducing its own carbon footprint, aiming to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, thereby contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate goals. The Monetary Authority is advancing environmental sustainability while upholding its commitment to safeguarding employee well-being, promoting financial inclusion, and fulfilling its social responsibilities. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is committed to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA puts the principles of sustainable development into practice across three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee is responsible for leading the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. The Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority and includes three Deputy Chief Executives, as well as representatives from the Risk Management and Supervision Department and the Institutional Development and Operations Department. It submits regular reports to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the leadership of the committee, multiple teams and working groups were tasked with planning and implementing measures within their respective areas of responsibility. In 2022, the Corporate Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved the institution's climate objectives and reviewed the transition roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to monitor the progress of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) green initiatives, including proposals to strengthen the HKMA's sustainable procurement policy, procedures, and methodologies. Sustainable Governance Framework: For its sustained commitment to environmental stewardship, employee well-being, and the broader community, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been awarded the "15+ Years of Caring Together" logo by the Hong Kong Council of Social Service for the 16th consecutive year. The Monetary Authority is deeply committed to monitoring its own carbon footprint and has established internal "Green Office Guidelines" to manage the environmental impact of its operational procedures. The Monetary Authority has integrated environmental considerations into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, the Green Building Council (GBI) awarded the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) a Gold certification for certain renovated office areas under its BEAM Plus scheme. This is the second green building certification, following the LEED Gold certification received in 2021. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has implemented a range of energy-saving measures, earning the "Green Building Mark" Gold rating for its interior architecture under the 1.0 version. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per capita), representing a 24.4% decrease from 2015 (Figure 1). In 2022, total greenhouse gas emissions from Scopes 1 and 2 amounted to 2,996.4 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e), or 1.7 tCO2e per capita, representing a 38.2% reduction compared to 2015 levels (Figure 2). Figures 1 and 2: Greenhouse gas emission intensity (Scopes 1 and 2). The Monetary Authority encourages institutions to adopt paperless internal operations. In addition, the Monetary Authority has implemented a print management system requiring staff to log in to printers to confirm each print request, thereby helping to reduce unnecessary printing and toner consumption. If printing is indeed necessary, we encourage the use of double-sided paper and black-and-white printing. The Monetary Authority is also preparing to implement an internal electronic records retention system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 metric tons (0.0114 metric tons per capita), representing a 65.3% decrease compared to 2015 (Figure A). Figure A: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's waste management continues to adhere to the "4R" principle. In addition to traditional waste, the HKMA has also reduced e-waste by adopting technical solutions such as server virtualization and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the Monetary Authority engaged an external firm for the first time to conduct a waste audit, analyzing the composition of waste generated in its offices. The audit revealed that food waste constitutes a significant portion of total waste, prompting the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong to launch a food waste recycling initiative (see page 41, "Strengthening Waste Management"). The total volume of non-hazardous waste generated in 2022, comprising both general and recyclable waste, amounted to 242.0 metric tons (0.135 metric tons per capita), representing a 4.8% decrease compared to 2015 (Figure 3). The fluctuations in the trend were primarily attributable to remote work arrangements implemented during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations following the fifth wave of infections. Figure 3: Density of non-hazardous waste. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) prioritizes waste prevention at the source and is committed to reducing, reusing, and recycling. In 2022, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) engaged a firm for the first time to conduct a waste audit, aiming to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste generated in daily operations—including plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood, and electronic products—and to provide recommendations for waste reduction. Based on the audit findings, the Monetary Authority launched a food waste recycling program in November, installing food waste collection bins in all pantry areas. Daily collected kitchen waste is transported to an organic resource recycling center in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy for electricity generation. Residues generated during the conversion process can also be composted for landscape enhancement and agricultural production. Additionally, recycling bins are installed at various locations throughout the office for convenient use. The Monetary Authority shared recycling tips with staff and placed greater emphasis on further improving source separation of recyclables, as well as on best practices for handling recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles. In addition, we continue to organize activities to enhance employees' environmental awareness, explain our waste management policies, and encourage the effective use of recycling facilities in the office. Daily collected kitchen waste is transported to Organic Resource Recovery Centres for plastic recycling. The Monetary Authority of Hong Kong operates two data centres: one for active operations and one as a backup. Given that these two areas account for the majority of the institution's total energy consumption, the HKMA has implemented green design principles and a range of energy-saving measures, including cabinet-type air conditioning systems, LED lighting, and 24-hour monitoring of electricity efficiency. Following the completion of the aforementioned consultant study on the green performance of the data center in 2022, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is now preparing to implement recommendations aimed at enhancing overall energy efficiency. Additionally, preparations have begun for obtaining Green Data Centre certification. The Monetary Authority of Singapore recognizes the importance of cultivating a sustainable development culture and, accordingly, regularly launches various initiatives and activities to educate and encourage staff to adopt habits conducive to sustainability, as well as to embrace green and digital working practices. The Monetary Authority shared practical tips on green living and presented the office's annual statistics on energy consumption and paper usage, reminding staff of the importance of individual actions in addressing environmental challenges. It also encouraged employees to submit suggestions on sustainability matters. Under the leadership of a senior manager from the Administrative Division, a task force comprising employees from various departments convened to brainstorm and develop ideas and concrete measures for fostering a green workplace. Members of the special working group also serve as ambassadors when launching new green initiatives. The Monetary Authority encourages the broader society to adopt more environmentally friendly practices and has introduced a range of measures to enhance operational efficiency within the Authority, the financial sector, and the economy as a whole, while minimizing resource consumption. The Monetary Authority of Singapore's "Submission of Electronic Forms and Tables" (STET) system is a one-stop platform enabling banks to submit documents electronically to the MAS, covering all periodic reports required on a weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annual basis. Another "Electronic Delivery" (e-Delivery) system is a secure electronic communication channel that enables the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to issue notices, guidelines, and other information to banks. Both systems collectively save a significant amount of paper annually. In handling bank complaints and enforcement matters, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has implemented measures to support paperless document submission, enabling bank customers to lodge complaints via electronic channels and by completing online forms. The Monetary Authority is also developing a next-generation management information system to enhance complaint handling and facilitate the transition from paper-based records to digital records. To reduce paper usage, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) 9 has adopted digital signatures in its routine communications with participants, including the issuance of notices, account opening and closure letters, and responses to audit confirmations. Looking ahead, CMU will continue to explore additional green initiatives, including the adoption of automated electronic procedures for both internal communication and external engagement. The Monetary Authority has been promoting the adoption of the Faster Payment System "FPS" and stored-value payment instruments to encourage the public to use electronic payment methods more widely, in place of cash and physical cheques. Further information on "Faster Payment System" (FPS) and stored-value payment facilities is provided in the chapter "Hong Kong's Role as an International Financial Centre" of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Annual Report 2022. Distributing electronic red packets is simple and convenient, helps reduce the use of physical red packet envelopes and cash, and contributes to advancing Hong Kong's sustainable development. To this end, the Monetary Authority continues to actively promote through various social and traditional media platforms, encouraging residents to distribute electronic red packets via Faster Payment System (FPS) or other e-wallet services through online or mobile banking during the Lunar New Year period. Major banks and e-wallet operators are also launching a range of initiatives to encourage users to adopt digital red packets, such as introducing festive, Lunar New Year-themed user interfaces, enhancing functionality for greater convenience, and offering lucky draws and cashback rewards. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is promoting e-red packets on social media. For residents who still choose to distribute physical red packets during the Lunar New Year, MAS continues to encourage the use of "new-old" banknotes—crisp, freshly issued notes—for sealing the red packets. The issuance of commemorative notes can reduce the need to print new currency, thereby lessening the environmental impact. The feedback from the note-issuing banks indicates that the public has become increasingly accepting of the new banknotes in recent years. The coin collection initiative reflects the HKMA's efforts in promoting the recycling of coins. Coins collected through this scheme will be returned to circulation to meet public demand, enhance the efficiency of coin circulation, and reduce the need for new coin minting. The program operates two coin-collection vehicles and has, to date, served over one million passengers, collecting more than 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HK$1.3 billion. In 2022, approximately 78% of users chose to allocate some or all of their stored-value balance to top up their stored-value payment tool accounts. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has maintained a collaborative partnership with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service (HKCSS), deploying cash collection vehicles on Non-Governmental Organizations' Flag Day to collect coins, thereby demonstrating its commitment to supporting social services. Launched in 2014, the Coin Counting Machine and Coin Collection Program on the Cash-in-Transit Vehicle was the world's first systematic coin collection initiative based on the concept of a mobile vehicle. Over the years, it has received numerous local and international awards, and its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin processing has been widely recognized. The plan includes two collection carts, each equipped with two high-speed coin counters to gather coins exchanged by the public. Members of the public may choose to exchange their coins for banknotes, use them to add value to stored-value payment instruments (such as Octopus cards or e-wallets), or donate them to the Community Chest as charitable contributions. In addition to coin collection, the cashier car is also occasionally assigned to various educational activities, such as student visits.

The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency has independently verified the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) climate targets ("Climate Targets"). The climate targets have been established in accordance with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual ("SBTi Corporate Manual"). The purpose of this validation exercise is to verify whether the climate targets have been formulated in accordance with the SBTi Corporate Manual. This verification engagement was conducted in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements (ISAE) 3000 (Revised), "Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information," issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB). The verification process is designed to form an opinion and draw conclusions to provide a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process is conducted in accordance with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The Monetary Authority is responsible for the collection and reporting of data. Our verification work is absolutely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this validation, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Centre provides reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The climate targets were established in accordance with the SBTi Corporate Manual. Shen Xiaoyin, Audit Supervisor, certified the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency's March 2023 verification statement, which confirms the independent verification conducted by the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency on the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (the "HKMA") 2022 environmental data (the "2022 Data"). The 2022 data encompass total energy consumption for 2022, intensity metrics for Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, paper usage intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rate, along with the percentage changes in these indicators relative to 2015 baseline levels. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's greenhouse gas emission data were compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, jointly issued by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD). The scope of verification encompasses data related to the period from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2022, as well as comparative data from the period January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2015, used for annual performance benchmarking. The verification scope covers a total of six office and warehouse assets: four offices located at 1) International Finance Centre Phase 2, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) Taikoo Place Phase 1, and 4) Kowloon Trade Centre; and two warehouses situated at 5) Luen Shing Industrial Centre and 6) Chong Lei Centre, all in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The purpose of the validation is to provide reasonable assurance of the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 data and to confirm the adequacy of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's data collection mechanisms. Within the scope of verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Authority reviewed representative data and supporting evidence selected from six assets. This verification engagement was conducted in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements (ISAE) 3000 (Revised), "Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information," issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB). The verification process is designed to provide an opinion and conclusion that offers a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process is conducted in accordance with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tested the completeness and accuracy of the selected sample data by tracing it back to its source. It also reviewed the fundamental procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal controls, and conducted reliability testing. The verification process also included validating internal data collection and management mechanisms, conducting interviews with representatives responsible for preparing the 2022 data, and selecting representative data and information for review. The underlying raw data and supporting evidence were also thoroughly reviewed during the validation process. The Monetary Authority is responsible for data collection and reporting. Our verification work is absolutely independent and impartial. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency (HKQAA) verification team did not participate in the 2022 data preparation process. Based on the findings of this verification exercise, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance on the 2022 data and concludes that: • the 2022 data are substantially accurate and reliable; and • the overall data collection mechanism of the Monetary Authority is adequate. Sham Siu-yin served as an audit supervisor for the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency in March 2023.

Expanding and accelerating climate action has become the most urgent challenge of our time. The critical first decade of the climate crisis is now nearly half over. We need to cut global carbon emissions by more than 40% over the next decade to have a realistic chance of limiting global warming to 1.5°C. However, greenhouse gas emissions have continued to reach record highs. The latest climate science research indicates that the window to limit global temperature rise to 1.5°C is rapidly closing. The impacts of a 1.1°C rise in global temperatures are now clearly evident: record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding and storms, and other extreme weather events are occurring with increasing frequency and intensity across the globe. Hong Kong was no exception. In September last year, after being battered by a ferocious super typhoon, we were immediately followed by a century-defining downpour. Despite our robust infrastructure and rapid disaster response capabilities, the impact remains severe, with widespread flooding, traffic disruptions, and damage to numerous roadways. All of this serves as a clear reminder that resolute and proactive climate action is urgently needed. Asia faces particularly significant challenges on its path toward low-carbon transformation, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that appropriately balance climate action with economic growth and social inclusion. This is by no means an easy task. Due to the region's rapid economic growth and fast-rising population, its carbon emissions account for more than half of global total emissions. At the same time, the Asia-Pacific region, with its high population density and geographic location, is particularly vulnerable to the impacts of rising sea levels and extreme weather events. Given the divergent stages of economic development within the region, while the low-carbon transition presents new opportunities for some economies, it poses a formidable challenge for others in mobilizing the necessary funding for transformation. Market estimates indicate that Asia-Pacific countries will require annual low-carbon transition investments exceeding $3 trillion over the next 30 years. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong has both the capacity and the responsibility to harness the power of finance to support low-carbon transition across the entire Asian region. As a banking regulator, market enabler, and responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has made significant contributions to the sustainable development agenda. Readers will be able to gain insight into the various specific measures and initiatives launched by the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong over the past year through the individual chapters of this report. In addition, to strengthen the internal governance framework of the HKMA and to enhance the coordination of sustainable development efforts across different functional areas, we established the Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee last year. For detailed information on the Supervisory Committee, please refer to the newly added section titled "Governance for Sustainable Development." Hong Kong banks play a pivotal role in supporting Asia's transition to net zero emissions. In addition to fulfilling the traditional functions of banking regulators, we ensure that banks effectively manage climate risks through our day-to-day supervisory activities. We also play a facilitator role, supporting the banking sector in providing financing for the transition to a low-carbon economy. One example is the development of a green taxonomy to assist banks and other financial institutions in identifying environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate objectives. We launched a prototype of our Green Classification Framework for consultation in May and are currently refining the framework based on feedback received during the consultation period. Furthermore, as there is growing demand for higher-quality sustainability disclosure information that is comparable on a global scale, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is working with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong, adopting the disclosure standards released by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) in June, which constitute a comprehensive set of global baseline standards for sustainability reporting. As a facilitator, the HKMA's role extends beyond establishing frameworks and regulations; we are also committed to addressing pain points faced by the industry. Currently, many banks are constrained by limited data, making it difficult to conduct substantive risk assessments. In light of this, the HKMA will launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform in the near term. Banks will be able to simply input a property address to assess the impact of physical climate-related hazards on Hong Kong's residential and commercial buildings under various climate scenarios, thereby assisting banks in managing associated climate risks. As Asia's premier international financial centre and a sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has consistently served as a bridge, channeling international investment into Asia's sustainable development projects and supporting the region's low-carbon transition. In recent years, the total volume of international green and sustainable bonds issued in Hong Kong has accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, clearly outperforming other regions. Particularly noteworthy is that, for the third consecutive year, the Shenzhen Municipal Government, and for the second consecutive year, the Hainan Provincial Government, issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong in 2023, further underscoring Hong Kong's pivotal role as a green gateway connecting mainland China with the rest of the world. The vibrant growth of the sustainable bond market in Hong Kong has been partly driven by the demonstration effect of the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has assisted the Government in issuing approximately USD 25 billion in green bonds, which were sold to both institutional and retail investors. We seize every issuance opportunity to continuously innovate and expand the features of green bonds, including currencies, tenors, and distribution channels, thereby laying a solid foundation for other public and private green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world's largest government retail green bond in 2022, we issued the world's first tokenized government green bond in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the issuance of the second tranche of tokenized green bonds. Priced in four major currencies and issued in a digitally native format, these bonds represent the world's first multi-currency digital green bonds. At the same time, we have proactively introduced a range of measures to enhance the vitality and competitiveness of Hong Kong's sustainable finance ecosystem. This encompasses work across multiple domains, including skills training, data improvement, green fintech, and transition finance. In particular, regarding talent development, in 2023 we launched a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the Banking Competency Framework, offering systematic training to banking professionals to enhance their understanding and expertise in green and sustainable finance. Transition finance is another key focus area for us; it provides funding for decarbonization initiatives in high-emission and hard-to-abate sectors, ensuring these industries do not face stalled transitions due to a lack of financial support. To support the robust development of transition finance, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong will expand the local Green Taxonomy to cover transition activities. We will also expand the scope of the Green and Sustainable Finance Credit Guarantee Scheme (GFS) to include transition bonds and loans, thereby encouraging enterprises in the region to raise transition financing in Hong Kong. Furthermore, we will strengthen communication and engagement with relevant stakeholders, leveraging public-private partnerships and blended finance models to attract private sector investment into sustainable development projects that have historically faced financing challenges. The aforementioned work requires cross-sector collaboration and is primarily coordinated by the Cross-sector Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, co-chaired by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional cooperation is equally important. In addition to our long-term collaboration with the International Finance Corporation on the Green Banking Alliance, the Infrastructure Finance Promotion Office of the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSB) joined the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance and the Partnership for Green Development Financing as founding members in 2023. Additionally, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ) has announced plans to establish a regional office in Hong Kong. Through these partnerships, we aim to foster skills development and knowledge sharing, thereby directing capital toward sustainable projects within our region and around the globe. To advance new business development and facilitate knowledge exchange, the Monetary Authority also co-hosted the inaugural Hong Kong Green Week earlier this year, attracting over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 regions. These included top decision-makers from the global business and finance sectors, who convened to discuss strategies for scaling up regional climate finance and to forge new partnerships in this area. At the Hong Kong Green Week flagship event, the Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum, Mr. Yu Wei-man, Chief Executive, delivered a speech emphasizing that, as the manager of Hong Kong's official foreign exchange reserves and a major global asset owner, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority must lead by example and act as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has led the way in green and sustainable asset investment, progressively expanding the Exchange Fund's portfolio of ESG and green assets in both public and private markets. In support of the Exchange Fund's Investment Portfolio's goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) launched last year a new active global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition, and expanded the application of a customised low-carbon equity index to another public market asset portfolio. Furthermore, the green, social, and sustainable development bonds that the Monetary Authority prioritizes for investment have outperformed their benchmark, underscoring the principle that doing good can also lead to financial success. In the private markets, we continued to pursue green-related investment opportunities and became anchor investors in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. As of the end of 2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio decreased by 6% and 46% compared to its 2021 and 2017 levels, respectively, and remained below the overall market average. As a sustainable institution, the Monetary Authority of Singapore will continue to strive for progress by formulating our sustainability goals and plans on the foundation of three core pillars: environmental stewardship, employee well-being, and social responsibility. Specifically, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has continually strengthened its capacity to address climate change throughout its low-carbon transition journey by assessing our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures encompass emissions reductions, improved energy efficiency, and waste management, ultimately aiming to fulfill our commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We have established a plan to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions in the short term and are making strong progress toward our interim 2030 target for reducing Scope 2 emissions. To attract and retain top talent and fulfill the HKMA's key functions, the Authority is committed not only to achieving its green targets but also to promoting the physical and mental well-being of its employees.
